text: A penny for Pep Guardiola’s thoughts. The legendary Manchester City manager was back at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since his departure at the end of last season and, well, the announcement of you-know-what.

Sporting a flat cap, Guardiola took his seat in the stands behind the City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and the chief executive, Ferran “Not” Soriano, and, certainly, the TV director seemed intent on scrutinising him – if the number of cutaway shots to him were any guide.

Everybody knows where Guardiola stands on the great City scandal; the numerous guilty verdicts handed down to them on the 100-plus charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. He has backed his former employers to somehow disprove them. But what did he make of his old team here against the might of the defending European champions, Paris Saint-Germain?

Not much in the first half would have been a reasonable conclusion. PSG played football from a higher plane and might have led by more than the three unanswered goals they scored. But if defiance has been the theme for City – and it fed into Guardiola’s presence here – they produced plenty more of it during a wild second half.

City refused to accept the inevitable. They threw everything at PSG. Erling Haaland ran on adrenaline as City created a fistful of clear openings. Haaland finished with two goals and a couple of near misses. City were close to worrying PSG.

The problem for Enzo Maresca and his players was the goal from Maghnes Akliouche for 4-1. It was a blast from outside the area that Gianluigi Donnarumma appeared to have palmed up and away. Except that the ball dropped back down and into the net. PSG even had time to miss a late penalty from Ferran Torres; the kick was weak and too close to Donnarumma. Are you missing it all, Pep?

The City support booed the Uefa anthem, as usual, due to their long-standing grievances with the European governing body, albeit they have surely been overtaken by issues closer to home. Perhaps they can co-exist unhappily?

Their team’s idea had been to measure themselves against the best and there were reasons why PSG shimmered with such menace. One was that Luis Enrique’s starting XI featured seven players who are on the 30-strong Ballon d’Or shortlist. He had another three from it among his substitutes, including João Neves and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

PSG were slick and sharp at the outset. There was the trademark assurance on the ball; the beautifully grooved combinations. It does not matter how tight the spaces are. They back themselves to get out of them. Witness the opening goal and a scintillating piece of team play that began deep on the right-hand side of their defensive third.

In the blink of an eye, PSG were surging up the flank and then opening out the move, Fabián Ruiz playing the final pass to Doué on the left. The winger cut inside and shot low for the near corner from outside the area. It was the precision that did for Donnarumma, although the former PSG goalkeeper had to do better at his post.

When PSG landed the follow-up punch just 75 seconds later, City were reeling, the home crowd stunned. The travelling PSG fans were beside themselves. It was a goal that featured two crosses, the first from Dembélé after some nice footwork out to Doué on the left. He took the ball down and crossed back for Dembélé, who had stolen in behind Marc Guéhi. The striker was unmarked; the run was too cute. Dembélé’s header was straightforward.

It was no exaggeration to say that PSG could have had five by the interval. City had no defence to their cut and thrust; the sheer pace of it. The positional fluidity, too. What was the right-back Achraf Hakimi doing marauding up the inside left? Causing major problems.

Hakimi popped up inside the six-yard box in the 32nd minute only to send a free header against the post but City were swiftly disabused of the notion that the danger had passed. Almost immediately, PSG seized on a lofted Donnarumma clearance and went for the jugular. Akliouche was involved and Warren Zaïre-Emery got the assist with a lovely backheel. Vitinha lashed a low drive home. The PSG support turned their backs on the pitch to perform a perfectly synchronised Poznan. It was a Parisian spectacle on and off the pitch. When Hakimi blew a one-on-one with Donnarumma on 39 minutes, his team were toying with City.

Maresca made a triple change at the interval, introducing Matheus Nunes, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye; an acknowledgement of how the first period got away from his team. The pickings in attacking terms had been slim. Antoine Semenyo blazed high at 0-0 after Matvei Safonov punched a corner against his own crossbar but there appeared to have been a foul on the PSG goalkeeper. There was not a great deal else from City.

They were better after the restart, playing with abandon. Semenyo crackled to life. Enzo Fernández blew a gilt-edged headed opportunity and Ndiaye worked Safonov before Haaland pulled one back. It was a whipped ball in from the inside left by Ndiaye, which Haaland redirected into the far corner with a flex of the neck muscles. He was not close in, either.

Could City take the lifeline? Semenyo ran through and dinked against the crossbar. The offside flag was raised, although he looked to have been level. City needed the next goal to make it interesting. Instead, they lost the initiative after another Donnarumma lapse.

text: Liverpool cleansed themselves from the stains of defeat by Manchester City at the earliest opportunity. A rampant display in Austria saw Bradley Barcola ignite his Liverpool account with the first hat-trick of his professional career and Andoni Iraola’s team devastate Lask’s big night in the Champions League. The major surprise was how the hosts managed to score three.

Iraola’s pre-match faith in the big-money signings Barcola and Florian Wirtz was repaid as the pair helped dismantle limited opponents. But it was not all about the money and the £123m signing from Paris Saint-Germain scoring the first goals of his Liverpool career. Lewis Koumas registered his first goal in the competition and replaced Steven Gerrard as the youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League game for Liverpool. A total of 26 shots equalled Liverpool’s record in a Champions League away game.

“I’m really happy for Bradley,” said the Liverpool head coach. “Yesterday you were asking me a lot about his numbers, and also Flo [Wirtz], and both of them played really well. They made a difference. Apart from the hat-trick Bradley was a threat one-v-one, helped us control the game and defended the pockets. It will do their confidence good for sure.”

The home end was full and in strong voice over an hour before kick-off as Lask supporters came to savour their club’s first home game in the Champions League proper. The Lask team proved to be much less impressive though, in fairness to the Austrian crowd, their support rarely wavered even as a rout unfolded before their eyes. Liverpool revelled in their superiority and the invitation to recover from Sunday’s first defeat of the season.

Iraola rested Virgil van Dijk, delaying the defender’s 200th game as Liverpool captain, and Alexis Mac Allister as he managed workloads ahead of Saturday’s visit to Brentford. A new-look central defence of Ronald Araújo and Jérémy Jacquet were given a physical test by the Lask strikers Samuel Adeniran and Krystof Danek but handled the host’s rudimental approach comfortably.

Liverpool were utterly dominant against an opponent that struggled to retain possession in all areas of the pitch. The breakthrough was inevitable but also a result of a mix-up in the Lask defence between Alemão and the goalkeeper, Lukas Jungwirth. From the second corner that followed their error, Araújo towered above his marker to head home Kostas Tsimikas’s delivery. It was the Uruguay international’s first Liverpool goal and the start of an onslaught.

Merely 96 seconds later it was 2-0 as Barcola also scored his first Liverpool goal. The summer recruit found himself under scrutiny ahead of the game, along with Wirtz, having gone six appearances for his new club without a goal or an assist. That issue was put to bed when Rio Ngumoha weaved in from the right and Koumas laid the ball back to the lurking winger. Barcola swept a first-time shot inside Jungwirth’s far post. Liverpool were enjoying themselves.

Wirtz soon found himself with a much-needed assist for Barcola’s second goal. The Germany international has looked more at home for Liverpool in the Champions League than Premier League and this was no exception. Wirtz picked out Barcola’s run into the Lask area and the winger rolled a cool finish beyond the exposed keeper.

Lask could have been seriously embarrassed before half-time. Koumas had a fine finish disallowed for offside and, following another neat exchange between Wirtz and Barcola, Ryan Gravenberch’s shot kissed the inside of the far post. Liverpool’s 19 attempts on goal were the most by an away side in the first half of a Champions League game since records began in 2003-04.

There would be no letup from Iraola’s team after the interval. Jeremie Frimpong morphed into an old-fashioned centre-forward to rise above Yvan Dibango and bury a textbook header into the bottom corner from Tsimikas’s cross. Koumas had a second goal disallowed for offside before Alisson’s clean sheet was ruined by the Lask substitute Robert Ljubicic sweeping home inside his near post. Barcola was presented with his hat-trick when Ngumoha released Frimpong and the full-back flashed a low cross through the Lask six-yard box. Barcola applied a simple finish at the back post.

Frimpong also supplied the assist for Koumas’s deserved goal, converted from close range after the home side were caught playing out from the back. The Lask substitute Florian Flecker brought a touch of respectability to the scoreline with two goals in four minutes, both set up by Dibango, but there was no disguising the emphatic manner of Liverpool’s victory nor the surge of confidence it should give to Barcola.

text: It may be a bit early for the pantomime season but the Holte End enjoyed acclaiming their heroes and villains as Aston Villa won at home for the first time this season in some style with their biggest European victory.

Every touch for Mason Greenwood, playing his first game in England in nearly five years, was booed, but even louder applause was reserved however for Aston Villa’s new-look attack. Switzerland international Johan Manzambi opened the scoring, celebrating his 21st birthday with a deflected shot in the 12th minute, before Nicolas Jackson put the game beyond Fenerbahce’s reach with two more goals before half-time.

Ibrahim Mbaye also contributed with a lively, pacy showing on the left wing. With Prince William cheering on from the stands, Ross Barkley made this a night to remember as he scored twice, the first goal from a penalty earned by Manzambi, to help banish any fears about playing in front of the demolished North Stand.

“Greenwood, Greenwood, what’s the score,” echoed around the three-quarters full Villa Park. Chants of a less salubrious nature were also given regular renditions. This was Greenwood’s first game in this country since he played in Manchester United’s 1-0 win against West Ham in January 2022.

Greenwood was charged in 2022 with attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour and assault occasioning actual bodily harm. The Crown Prosecution Service discontinued the case in February 2023 after key witnesses withdrew their involvement and new material came to light. The player had denied the charges.

He had played for Marseille in a friendly against Villa 15 months ago, when he allegedly spat at Amadou Onana and had a spat with Tyrone Mings. So it was no surprise when his name was booed as the teams were announced and at every subsequent involvement.

Far more palatable was the freedom with which Villa, who had previously failed to win at home this season, played, on a night when the pre-match claret and blue sparkles were matched by the fireworks. Jackson now has five goals for Unai Emery’s team since signing from Chelsea for £65m in the summer.
It was Manzambi who got the show on the road, composing himself to score his second goal for the club after Mattéo Guendouzi had inadvertently headed on John McGinn’s cross following a short corner.

Zion Suzuki twice saved well from Vedat Muriqi but Villa created umpteen chances themselves. Jackson, collecting Boubacar Kamara’s pass, struck home cleanly from the edge of the penalty area just after the half-hour mark before repeating the trick six minutes before the interval. In between, Oguz Aydin shot against the Villa bar, but, truth be told, Villa’s 11th successive home win in European competitions already looked safely banked.

Villa’s free-scoring spell is in stark contrast to their start to the season, when they only managed one goal in their opening four games. Now they have scored at least three times in four of their past six matches.
Should they beat Viking next Wednesday, as would be expected, Villa would be on their way to likely qualification.

So perhaps it was little surprise that the second half was played at training-ground pace for long spells. Villa had conceded four of their five goals in three previous winless home games in front of the empty North Stand, and seemed more intent on keeping a clean sheet for the second half than busting a gut to score.
Mbaye did sprint from one penalty area to the other, exchanging a one-two with Jackson en route, following a Fenerbahce corner before seeing his shot well saved.

Then Manzambi earned the penalty midway through the second half, when he was tripped by Ismail Yuksek, from which Barkley made it 4-0. The cheers that followed that were matched by the jeers for Greenwood as he was substituted. The pantomime was over as a contest, even if Barkley swiftly added a fifth with a deflected shot.

Suzuki, the home goalkeeper, had to tip over Aydin’s fierce shot five minutes from time but even before Tammy Abraham turned in Alysson’s cross for the sixth goal, Villa fans’ minds were starting to turn to Saturday evening’s trip to Newcastle United and the perennial autumnal challenge of resurrecting a difficult start to the league season. In Emery they trust.

news.desc: Specialist mentor signed lucrative deal with online firm Board’s strict code prohibits betting across cricket Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor. text: Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor. Pietersen signed a lucrative contract as a brand ambassador for an online gambling company this week.

The former England batter is contracted to work with Brendon McCullum’s white-ball team for around 150 days over the next 13 months until the conclusion of the 50-over World Cup co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Pietersen’s betting ­interests create a potential headache for his employers.

The ECB’s anti-corruption code bans participants from “directly or indirectly soliciting, inducing, enticing, instructing, persuading, encouraging, facilitating or authorising any other party to enter into a bet in relation to the result, progress, conduct or any other aspect of any match or competition.”

The ECB does not take advertising revenue from gambling companies, has banned Hundred franchises from sponsorship deals with betting firms from next year and its regulations state that any counties accepting commercial gambling income must demonstrate that the proceeds are reinvested into infrastructure projects or community programmes.

All participants in cricket are also prohibited from betting, a rule that led to the England fast bowler Brydon Carse being given a 16-month ban – 13 of which were suspended – two years ago for placing 303 bets between 2017 and 2019.

Pietersen announced he is joining the Philippines-based Dafabet on Monday. The 46-year-old is understood to have reassured the ECB, however, that he will not promote Dafabet while on England duty, which given the extent of his commitments over the next year will prove restrictive.

While Pietersen is not travelling to Pakistan for a 50-over tri series also featuring Sri Lanka that starts next week, he will play a full part in the winter tours of Australia and South Africa, as well as all England’s domestic white-ball matches next summer leading into the World Cup.

The ECB previously had issues regarding McCullum’s betting interests after the then Test coach joined the Cyprus-based company 22bet as an ambassador three years ago. He went on to promote its Indian Premier League betting markets on Facebook and YouTube.

The ECB concluded that McCullum was not in breach of its anti-corruption code, although he opted to terminate his relationship with 22bet anyway. Unlike 22bet, which is licensed offshore in Curacao, Dafabet has a licence to operate in the UK.

text: From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst

After Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez teed off at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox] … Really poor [the Atlético defeat] – I have to control myself a lot but something is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Here we consider the key questions emerging from Martínez’s explosive remarks.

Yes is the short answer. The Guardian has been told the decision to target three midfielders in Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba caused bemusement in the squad that no other areas were strengthened in the summer. Carrick led United to third last term after the side only had 17 league games remaining when he took over in January, having been eliminated from the other competitions. The need for defensive reinforcements is particularly acute because the back four of Diogo Dalot, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw has been together since 2022. Martínez is out of contract next summer and it is thought the 28-year-old may not be offered a new deal or have his one-year option triggered by the club, so teammates are conscious his outburst also came because he expects to leave.

As United’s director of football the 55-year-old wields near-unilateral power on football decisions, with only Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, above him. If the buck stops with the executive, the most recent transfer window was Wilcox’s responsibility. This was the latest in a line of missteps on his United record. One concerns when Dan Ashworth (Wilcox’s predecessor) was on gardening leave from Newcastle in the first half of 2024, Wilcox interviewed potential replacements for Erik ten Hag before, oddly, deeming that the head coach should stay. The Dutchman signed a fresh contract but was sacked that autumn. Another involves Wilcox’s major falling out with the man he hired as the Dutchman’s successor, Ruben Amorim, after which the Portuguese said the director of football had told him he should change his favoured 3-4-3 shape. “I came here to be the manager of Manchester United – not to be the coach of Manchester United,” said Amorim, after a 1-1 draw at Leeds on 4 January (his job title was head coach). He was sacked the next day. Wilcox worked with Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, at Manchester City, where Berrada rose to become chief football operations officer, and Wilcox became academy director. Wilcox moved to Southampton and became director of football from summer 2023 until April 2024, when he joined United, having been identified by Berrada, so there is scrutiny of his experience at elite level.

The 45-year-old’s ability to prosper is related to the quality of Wilcox’s work, primarily in the market, so he cannot be solely responsible for a dire six points from six league games and two victories in all competitions all season. Yet by definition his role as head coach demands Carrick do the best with his resources, and that progress is made on the training ground. On matchdays there is scant excuse for United’s disjointedness, inferior running stats and inability, twice, to take advantage against 10 men: the 1-0 loss to City and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham. How is Carrick viewed by his players? According to Santos they back him. “We believe in the manager, we believe in the whole staff, we believe in [ourselves as] players,” he said after the Atlético game. “We are in a bad moment but we have to work to change this result.”.

For further evidence see Amad Diallo’s Snapchat post after the defeat by Atlético: “Fucking disgrace; I have no words.” So United have a World Cup-winner, Martínez, aiming shots at Wilcox and by implication Ratcliffe and Berrada, and a fellow senior player, Diallo, cursing but in ambiguous fashion, adding to the sense of meltdown at the club because it is unclear whether the “disgrace” meant the performance, Martínez’s diatribe, the squad his teammate referred to as not good enough, or something else. All of this is mirrored on the pitch, where United’s 671.4km run in the Premier League is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2 is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

In mitigation Wilcox can point to the six American siblings, who remain majority owners and whose family has placed an eye-watering £1.1bn-plus debt on the club that severely restricts the transfer budget. Wilcox oversaw a £155m summer outlay and a net spend of about £100m in a summer when City’s corresponding figures were £457.5m and about £175m. City buying players such as Enzo Fernández (for a British record-equalling £125m), Elliot Anderson (£115m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£65m) showed their greater financial muscle, helped by being much better sellers of talent. How they have reached this point has, though, been thrown into sharp focus by last month’s verdict that they have serially cheated.

Any straw should be clutched at so Carrick and his staff can view the first 97 minutes of Baleba’s United career as a rosy augury. After entering on 59 minutes against Spurs, a cute swivel and deft chip to Bruno Fernandes was a moment as impressive as the rest of his debut, and at Atlético the 22-year-old hunted down opponents and crunched into tackles, suggesting his game contains energy, muscularity and skill. It’s early days but perhaps if Baleba had been fit to start the campaign (he was recovering from an ankle problem) he might have affected one or more of the defeat at Hull, the 2-2 draw at Everton when Ainsley Maitland-Niles equalised late, the 1-0 loss to City when Phil Foden was sent off after 23 minutes or the Carabao Cup elimination by Brighton.

news.title: Gianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meeting
news.desc: World Cup sell-off, Balogun and peace prize on agenda Opponents will press home need for independent review Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan , the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday. text: Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday.

The Fifa president rejected repeated calls for an extraordinary general meeting of council in the summer after the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposals, but will meet his critics for the first time since then in Zurich, with one attender predicting that the talks could be “explosive”.

Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani and Sheikh Salman Bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the presidents of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation respectively, all of whom have called for Infantino to resign, will be present to press home demands for an independent review of Fifa’s governance.

In response to letters from Ceferin, Montagliani and Salman sent last month Infantino pledged to commission an external review of Fifa’s future governance, but no details have been forthcoming, and there is scepticism over whether it will be truly independent.

In addition to FFE, Balogun and the peace prize, which featured on an agenda circulated by Fifa last month, Infantino is also likely to face questions about a report in the Times this week that he received a “second salary” of about £1.3m in 2024, on top of the £3.9m declared in Fifa’s accounts.

US Internal Revenue Service filings show a Fifa subsidiary in charge of running last summer’s World Cup paid Infantino $1.76m, that was not mentioned in Fifa’s annual report, in which his salary is recorded as 4.27m Swiss francs (£3.86m).
Fifa statutes state that “the individual compensation of the Fifa president … shall be made public”. The governing body has denied wrongdoing.

“Fifa does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation,” it said. “The Fifa president’s annual compensation, as well as other contractual benefits, are decided by the independent compensation subcommittee.

“Fifa strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes. Fifa accounts are independently audited, and all declarations are in line with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere.”

Despite these controversies, and the public opposition of the European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations, Infantino is on course to be re-elected unopposed in March’s election.

Montagliani has rejected calls to stand against Infantino to focus on being re-elected as Concacaf’s president and Uefa has yet to find an alternative candidate despite tentatively sounding out high-profile footballing figures including Arsène Wenger and Michele Kang, who owns clubs including London City Lionesses.
The deadline for candidates to declare their intention to stand is 18 November, with the election due to be held at Fifa congress in Rabat on 18 March.

Infantino is expected to put forward a £2.6bn increase in the amount of money Fifa hands out for global football development at the meeting in Zurich, using cash from the governing body’s reserves to do so. The hike, covering funding from 2027 to 2030, would take the total Fifa spend on football development for the period to £4.83bn.

text: Organisations such as 180 Project and Prison Run are helping to prepare prisoners for release with a fresh view on life on the outside

On the day 700 prisoners in England and Wales were released early, I was driving to Wolverhampton for an event organised by the not-for-profit group ConnectSport. It was to celebrate local sports clubs and initiatives that “help young people believe in themselves and realise what they’re capable of” as described by Ranjit Singh, a local legend in the world of wrestling, martial arts and Kabaddi.

I listened to several news cycles that detailed the risks of early release pitched against the intractable challenge of insufficient prison capacity. It was presented as a hopeless logjam with no solutions. Tagging was the only option mentioned as a way of reducing reoffending rates.

There is clearly no single solution, but it is an area where sport can and does make a difference and could do in a greater way, particularly if we start to see sport as more than a source of entertainment or physical fitness.

In his annual report, Charlie Taylor, HM chief inspector of prisons for England and Wales, emphasised the serious need to improve prisoners’ access to gyms and physical activity. Where it works, it works powerfully.

Twenty-five prisons and young offender institutions organise parkrun and research shows a range of benefits, including better mental and physical health; improved self-esteem and confidence; increased sense of purpose and achievement; and the creation of a safe, humanising and non-judgmental space in which to be active, feel valued and respected. All crucial factors that contribute to rehabilitation and reduced reoffending.

The former triathlete Chrissie Wellington, the Ironman world champion, is leading a new initiative, Prison Run, to train 20 men and women from three prisons, all nearing release, to run the 2027 London Marathon. Most will never have run more than a few miles. A group of mentors will coach them from their first run to marathon distance in prison, on temporary release days and post-release. They plan to bolster fitness programmes inside prison and provide support for life outside prison by connecting sport, mentoring, employment and community.

John McAvoy, a Nike-sponsored triathlete who broke world indoor rowing records while in prison for armed robbery, will be part of the coaching team. McAvoy describes Prison Run as a chance to “break the cycle” where 67.1% of adults released from sentences of less than 12 months reoffend.

Sport transformed McEvoy’s life and gave him a purpose, a community and a burning belief that the past does not have to define the future. He is driven to share it with others. “Everyone deserves a second chance,” he says. “Sometimes they just need someone to believe in them and I will as I run alongside them during this special event.”

Sport and physical activity can contribute to the much-needed pathway “through the gate” that is so broken. Highly praised by Taylor, 180 Project engages prisoners in CrossFit and connects them to a community when they come out with housing, life-coaching and other vital support services linked around the gym.

The project leaders invited me to run an indoor rowing masterclass. I met a group of motivated prisoners in their last year or so behind bars, hungry for tips to improve their scores and know what 500m splits to aim for on the rowing machine. Most crucially, they were building a new, common language, positive behaviours and a fresh perspective on life and community that could lead to a different future path.

One of the prisoners who left four months ago had been in and out of prison from the age of 15 and found more than fitness through 180 Project. He describes becoming part of a community and family of people “all dealing with something” and credits this project with “building my own self-awareness, becoming a better person to see the potential that’s inside”.
Lindsey Middleton, the inspiration co-founder of 180 Project, told me “people get physically, mentally, emotionally well and socially connected” through what they do.

It is an area where the UK has been building world-leading expertise. The Alliance of Sport in Criminal Justice connects local sports organisations with academics and government partners for a clearer understanding of how sport can help reduce crime.

Under James Mapstone’s leadership the alliance has gained a global reputation leading to a request to produce a youth crime prevention initiative across south-east Asia for the International Olympic Committee, funded by the French Development Agency.

The project aims to support 82,000 young people through 11 projects in Laos, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. Across the region, sport is being taken seriously as a tool to prevent youth crime and strengthen community resilience.
This work has been a priority for Kirsty Coventry since she became the IOC president and chose to emphasise sport’s role in fostering safer and stronger communities.

A recent poll from Forward Trust, a charity that supports people to recover from addiction and leave crime behind, showed strong public support for the use of rehabilitation programmes. The current crisis offers a moment where sport and physical activity could contribute to that on a bigger scale through its ability to influence communities, shape identities, work with government and other public authorities while adapting to local needs.

These ideas aren’t new. Prof Rosie Meek, a chartered psychologist and prison scholar at Royal Holloway, University of London has been researching the positive effect of sport and physical activity in prisons for more than 20 years.

Yet it remains underutilised. The role of sport and physical activity within prison life is overdue an update in order to understand the broader developmental and social benefits beyond physical fitness.

Outside, there is great scope to develop sport’s contributions to social challenges across our communities. Wellington has pledged through Prison Run to use sport to replace stigma with real stories of resilience, potential and second chances. Imagine a world where that becomes a proud part of sport’s contribution to the country.

text: The three-time world champion Jillaroos maintain a strong edge but their title defence may be under threat from New Zealand and England

Four years is a long time in women’s sport. While men’s sport is ever evolving and growing, the speed of change in the women’s game is much faster, as time lost when they were sidelined in professional sport at an increasingly rapid pace is made up.

The last time the Rugby League World Cup was held, the women’s game was in a very different place. The NRLW contained just six teams, playing five rounds of competition, which was positioned almost as a sideshow to the men’s finals. Since then, it has doubled in size to 12 teams and 11 rounds, getting genuine airtime across the Australian winter.

Women’s State of Origin has also grown to a three-match series, attracting crowds of over 20,000 and broadcast reach of over two million viewers per match. While this growth certainly benefits Australia, it has also strengthened women’s rugby league across the world.

Current NRLW players feature across the majority of teams in the 2026 World Cup – not just the Jillaroos. With double the number of players in the NRLW, it has not only provided opportunities for international players to take part, but also opened pathways for Australian players from different cultural backgrounds to represent the countries their parents and grandparents hail from. While this has long been common in men’s rugby league, having more players in the NRLW provides more visibility for those players to be seen and recruited by overseas coaches for the World Cup.

Although the Jillaroos remain favourites to back up their 2022 win, in which they defeated New Zealand 54-4 in the final, the gap is closing and this is shaping up to be the closest World Cup in history. Eight teams will compete for the title – five of those return from the 2022 iteration, Australia, New Zealand, England, Papua New Guinea and France. Fiji and Wales will make their first women’s Rugby League World Cup appearances, while Samoa will compete for the first time since 2003.

Most likely to challenge the Jillaroos are New Zealand and England. The Kiwi Ferns boast a full squad of NRLW players, most notably Canberra Raiders and former Queensland Maroons halfback Zahara Temara and Sydney Roosters premiership-winning prop Otesa Pule. England have strong experience in the Super League, including nine players from the dominant Wigan Warriors. They are bolstered by the inclusion of a number of NRLW stars, with Roosters second rower Jasmin Strange certain to make a big impact.

Where the Jillaroos maintain a strong edge, though, is in the combinations they have across the team. Their squad features eight players from the Roosters – undefeated NRLW premiers in 2026 – and 13 players from the NSW Sky Blues, who won the 2026 State of Origin series in a 3-0 whitewash. Not only have these players trained and played in these combinations throughout the year, they are highly experienced at winning together. The importance of this critical mass of players coming from a strong winning culture cannot be underestimated. In high-pressure games, a team who expects to win and plays with that mindset is difficult to beat.

The Jillaroos squad also has plenty of depth, and coach Jess Skinner will have some tough decisions to make before selecting her team for the big games in this tournament. The most intriguing battle is between the two halfbacks in the squad – State of Origin-winning half Jesse Southwell and NRLW premiership-winning half Tarryn Aiken. Both are incredible talents with the ability to turn the game to their advantage. Aiken’s more recent success gives her the edge – and she has been named at halfback for the opening match against Samoa – but expect Skinner to test both players throughout the tournament.

Roosters’ and Sky Blues’ five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher has been named to make her Australian debut in the opener and is likely to hold down that spot throughout the tournament, after outstanding performances in the NRLW and State of Origin series. Her kicking game is a key strength the Jillaroos will be seeking to exploit – her pinpoint accuracy was on show in the NRLW grand final, as she troubled the opposition kick chasers and set up multiple tries for her team with her fifth tackle options. Also working in Kelleher’s favour is her combination with both Aiken at the Roosters and Southwell in the Sky Blues’ set up.

Possibly the most controversial selection call for the Jillaroos has already been made, with former captain Ali Brigginshaw missing out on selection in the squad. Brigginshaw retired from the NRLW after this year’s grand final and, after missing out on a fairytale ending with the Brisbane Broncos, would have been hoping to end her career on a high with a World Cup win. But the selectors did not have the 36-year-old in their plans and she has been left to watch the tournament unfold from the stands, while Sky Blues’ and Sydney Roosters’ captain Isabelle Kelly takes the leadership reins.

“But this is football. Sometimes mistakes can happen; it’s life.“

news.title: Real Madrid's Vinicius Jr banned for four games and will miss El Clasico vs. Barcelona
news.desc: The Brazilian winger was sent off during the last home game against Villarreal after pulling Nathan Saliba's hair before scoring
text: Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr. will miss El Clasico against FC Barcelona on Oct. 25 after being suspended for four games for the red card he received in Real Madrid's last home game, against Villarreal at the Bernabeu. The Brazilian forward came on in the 52nd minute and was sent off 20 minutes later. Vinicius Jr. thought he had scored, and Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho celebrated alongside his team and ran over to him a few seconds before VAR ruled out the goal and sent him off. The VAR check showed Vinicius Jr. had pulled Nathan Saliba's hair before scoring. The Spanish Football Federation's rules state that pulling an opponent's hair is violent conduct, and Vinicius was suspended for the upcoming four Real Madrid matches against Sevilla, Barcelona, Racing Santander and Valencia. The federation's competition committee gave Vinicius a two-game ban for "violent conduct, without the possibility of playing the ball" and two additional games "for arguing with the referee with an aggressive attitude and having to be restrained by his teammates." Mourinho, who skipped Saturday's post-match press conference after the episode, spoke ahead of the Champions League match against AS Roma on Wednesday and said, "After the previous match against Atletico Madrid in which Vinicius started, I decided to take a different approach and to protect him a little and then bring him on when the game called for a player like Vini. I think that worked out well: the stadium, which had sometimes voiced disapproval, immediately rallied behind him the moment he started warming up. I believe that was a crucial turning point for him. He came on and played very well, the goal and the sending off were a shame, of course, but it seemed like something clicked for him, reigniting that joy and reminding him of the kind of player he truly is." The ban applies only to domestic competitions, so Vinicius will be able to play against AS Roma on Wednesday, then against RB Leipzig and on Nov. 4 against AEK Athens. He will be eligible to play in LaLiga again only after the November international break, when Real Madrid meet Celta Vigo on Nov. 22.

news.title: U.S. Soccer to launch Arthur M. Blank Crest Cup for women's clubs; initial prize pool set at $1.5 million
news.desc: There is currently no launch date for the Crest Cup but U.S. Soccer hopes to have the competition up and running before the 2031 Women's World Cup, which is expected to take place in North America
text: U.S. Soccer will launch the Arthur M. Blank Crest Cup, a first-of-its-kind women's competition in the country that will see clubs across different leagues compete with each other for a prize pool of $1.5 million. There is currently no start date for the Crest Cup, but U.S. Soccer intends to have the competition up and running by the 2031 Women's World Cup, which will likely be hosted jointly by the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. Teams from the NWSL and the Gainbridge Super League will take part in the inaugural edition of the event, though other clubs could join the fold at some point. "It'll for sure be the NWSL teams and the GSL teams and we're looking at the option for lower division professional teams being able to join, as well as amateur women's teams being able to join and what that could and should look like but we're also not of the thought that the tournament can't evolve," U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone told select members of the media this week. "Maybe we start with the NWSL and GSL, and then evolve and engage the other teams, right?" The tournament will resemble the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup, the century-old men's club competition, and other similar cup competitions around the world such as the FA Cup. Parlow Cone admitted she had a longtime interest in launching a women's equivalent in the U.S. and has finally been able to follow through with the idea because of the increasingly robust nature of women's club soccer at the professional and amateur levels nationwide. "I have wanted to launch this competition for quite some time," Parlow Cone said. "Historically, we haven't had a robust women's amateur league and competition and a number of teams in order to do it and we only had the one Division One professional league, so it didn't seem like the right time then and now GSL has come in as another Division One league and as they get the first couple of years under their belt, I feel like now we're going to also help grow amateur women's soccer in our country so it felt like the right time. Also, as we gear up for the World Cup in 2031, I think this is great timing in order to create another competition." As with the Open Cup, the Crest Cup winner will be able to qualify for the Concacaf W Champions Cup, broadening experiences for players and staff alike. "Most of the players and the coaches and the teams in our ecosystem, they only get that international exposure if they make their national teams or if they're lucky, one or two teams, to be able to play in the Concacaf tournament but this is another way to get more players interleague competition that could then lead to international competition in really meaningful games, right?" she said. "Because single elimination, you got to perform on the given day or you're eliminated and then hopefully around the corner, this leads to being able to play in the Women's Club World Cup." It is likely that Crest Cup games will take place midweek, in between the weekend games that usually take up the calendar in the NWSL and the GSL, but Parlow Cone said it was too early to say definitively. Finding spots on the schedule to play Crest Cup games will be among U.S. Soccer's biggest challenges since player load is changing at the highest levels of the game. In the last two years alone, the inaugural editions of the Concacaf W Champions Cup and the FIFA Women's Champions Cup have been staged, while FIFA also intends to introduce a Women's Club World Cup. The latter competition is reportedly slated to take place in the U.S. in the winter of 2028, according to the Guardian, only adding to the new types of games players might face. On the flip side, players outside the NWSL run the risk of playing too few games - the 2026 GSL season, for example, runs from August to November and will only feature 14 regular-season matches. Parlow Cone said she is working in collaboration with both the NWSL and the GSL to find the right spots on the calendar while taking player load into consideration. "I'm a former player so this is always top of mind for me specifically," she said. "I've said it several times. We could not be working more closely with NWSL and GSL and their sporting leaders to create models for the schedules for the exact reason that you mentioned and we want to make sure that we're not overloading the players, not underloading and allowing enough recovery between their league matches and the Crest Cup matches so like I said before, I would imagine that this would be mostly midweek matches but I'm not gonna declaratively say that right now. We're not announcing a launch date, I'm definitely not telling you what day of the week we're gonna play the matches quite yet."

news.title: Ashley Sanchez makes her case as USWNT battle back for draw against Spain
news.desc: Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson scored to help the U.S. team claw their way out of a 2-0 deficit against the world champions
text: CHESTER, Pa. – The U.S. women's national team needed to start solidly against Spain on Tuesday, four days after the visitors took a two-goal lead in 14 minutes and never looked back. The steady start came but by the 32nd minute, the USWNT were in the same exact pickle. Two defensive lapses cost them against the reigning world champions and the USWNT were in need of a problem-solver with roughly an hour still left on the clock.
On a team that boasts several likely suspects, one finally emerged – Ashley Sanchez.
Ashley Sanchez scores in her first USWNT start in 714 days 💪 pic.twitter.com/gfHqyCJqIk

Sophia Wilson darted towards goal but with a defender inching closer, she sent the ball to her left. It slowly drifted towards Sanchez, who had the space to do whatever she wanted. She cut inside and entered the penalty area, unbothered by the two defenders in front of her who had otherwise proven to be up for the task of handling the U.S. team's historically capable offense. They left a crevice of space that only the most talented of players could exploit, Sanchez rising to the challenge effortlessly. The ball took a bounce near the goal line but she took the hit for a reason – no one was in a position to stop it and so it landed in the back of the net, just as she had intended.

The moment of brilliance is hardly a surprise from the NWSL's golden boot leader, the 27-year-old in the form of her life and as well-equipped as any to rattle an otherwise sturdy Spain back line. Sanchez had earned her spot in the starting lineup on Tuesday, the USWNT's most dynamic attacker a natural inclusion on a day they hoped to show the attacking end product that was missing in Saturday's loss. The overall results were mixed – the U.S. team still came out with a 2-2 draw, Spain the aggressors this time on a day where their attacking might was genuinely hard to miss. In Sanchez, though, the USWNT had a bright spot.

"Her experience, her maturity and the ability to be able to transfer knowledge," head coach Emma Hayes said post-match. "Even she said to me at the end, 'There's so much I still need to be able to do,' which is natural but I thought she did a great job. I'm really happy for her to get a goal."

Until Sanchez's goal, the USWNT had gone goalless in 139 minutes of play against Spain and not for a lack of effort. Finishing was an issue – they generated 2.26 expected goals without actually scoring, the issue exemplified in Lily Yohannes' missed penalty midway through the second half. Matters felt worse at halftime of Tuesday's defeat, the U.S. team only generating 0.23 expected goals from six shots. They were in desperate need of someone who would finally make a difference and Sanchez stepped up, both at a timely juncture for the team and for herself.

Sanchez had been out of the national team picture for two years until this month's friendlies, though her return had become undeniable by the time Hayes named the roster two weeks earlier. She had pulled off the feat after a position change at the North Carolina Courage, enjoying the best season of her career as a left winger after years of playing in midfield. Finding a way to impress against Spain would be another challenge entirely but one Sanchez ultimately embraced, making her case not a moment too soon.

"I think it felt natural, but obviously I think there's a little bit of, still, tactical adjustment that I need to have and because I haven't been here for that long," Sanchez said, reflecting on her first USWNT camp in two years. "It has only been a week. I know that I, defensively, could do a little bit better, so I think for me, that's my biggest takeaway. I'm really happy with the goal, but I think it did feel comfortable on the field with the connections that I have, but ultimately, I know I still have some [room for] improvement."

The Spain friendlies were always destined to test the USWNT's depth, especially without a few key players through injury, Sanchez adding to the narrative in all the right ways. She started in the place of Alyssa Thompson, who was amongst the positives on Saturday and still very much looks like a potential starter at the Women's World Cup in eight months' time. That spot on the left of Hayes' preferred three-person front line, though, is as competitive as any on a team that has aimed to have cover in just about every position on the pitch.

Hayes has a good type of problem on her hands in that position, if this week's games are anything to go by. How she picks between two talented players who seem poised to make a difference on good days and bad is one of the many questions that await over the next eight months, though in some ways it may not need answering. On days where the U.S. team's shortcomings are on display, particularly in defense without the injured Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey, that very specific type of depth might be the exact thing to bail Hayes' side out of trouble in a make-or-break situation.

Sanchez was hardly the only person to offer a reminder of the USWNT's historic dominance in attack. Mallory Swanson's 86th-minute equalizer marked her first goal for the national team since welcoming her daughter Josie nearly a year ago, the forward slowly working her way back into the group in just her second international game after maternity leave.

"I honestly thought Michelle [Cooper] was going to finish it, but the defender did well and recovered, and she made the right decision in the box, and I was just able to take a touch and come across my body and finish it."
Mallory Swanson scores her first USWNT goal since the Olympic gold medal match to bring them level 2-2 with Spain 😤 pic.twitter.com/4I4VC0oexv

It was vintage Swanson, her goal calling back to her crowning achievement thus far with the U.S. team. She played a central role in the gold medal run at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, scoring four goals, including the lone goal in the final against Brazil. In a week that was ultimately defined by the USWNT's inability to convert their chances, Swanson's goal was a welcome development for Hayes and company.

"I think Mal has shown improvement every day in training," Hayes said. "Didn't think she was quite ready for 45, so we did push, and I said to her, 'You've got another one in you at this level,' and she's in a better place to be able to perform more consistently, but I say it all the time -- she's an important player on our team, and I think the more we have her back, the better it'll get. I think she missed a big chance. It reminded me of the Olympic gold medal moment. I was like, 'This is the one player you want in this position,' and she lifted it, but she didn't miss the second one. That's what you have to do at this level, though. You don't get many. You got to finish them."

There is still time on the clock for the USWNT to fully flesh out their World Cup identity, while the job of actually qualifying for next summer's tournament in Brazil is technically still on the to-do list -- next month's Conccacf W Championship quarterfinal against El Salvador is essentially a win-and-in game. Hayes' embarrassment of riches in attack, though, might make up for the weaknesses in the back that were apparent over the course of both friendlies against Spain. Though the U.S. team played with a more traditional No. 6 in Claire Hutton on Tuesday, the defensive unit as a whole still succumbed to their opponent's attacking brilliance. The newness of the connections might be to blame, at least partially. Tierna Davidson and Kennedy Wesley only played their second game together at center back, while they had a different goalkeeper behind them this time in Phallon Tullis-Joyce.

"It's really important to be able to build a partnership, I think, especially as a center back partnership because it's not just like us having to do our jobs but it's a lot of us organizing forward," Davidson said. "To be able to kind of learn each other's tendencies and build that relationship is really important because I think going into tournaments, the strength of our team is our depth, so whatever combination of players that needs to be on the field for us to win, the more that you can have all of the relationships built, the better. So I think it's a really important thing for us to do in these types of games is to kind of be in those pressure moments and build, and honestly, sometimes it is making mistakes. Maybe it is we're not fully on the same page, but these are the moments to get that right."

Unseating Girma, arguably the game's best center back, is perhaps an unrealistic expectation for Wesley or anyone else technically in the running. By force or otherwise, though, Hayes continues to leave no stone unturned when it comes to actually handing players' experiences well before their major tournament debuts come around.

"We've got to develop a group and in one game, you're going to rely on one situation," Hayes said. "Another group, it might be another. The importance is the whole pack, especially in a game where you've got eight subs. At a World Cup, don't know what the sub pattern will be but the benches are critical. Gone are the days of an 11. That's finished in top flight football so I always wonder why people keep asking, 'What's the settled 11 going to be?' That's a story of the past in football. You're never going to always have your best players available because of whatever reason -- injury, form -- so you have to have enough who know how to play and the same with Spain. Spain still maximized eight subs. They've got a whole development system where they can slip one out, one in. Seamless. Doesn't matter if they're missing some of their best players. They demonstrated in two games why they're world champions so we have to get up to that level."

news.title: What to watch in UEFA Champions League: All eyes on Manchester City vs PSG; Real Madrid face big test at Roma
news.desc: Enzo Maresca's side faces the ultimate tactical test against back-to-back champions PSG, while Jose Mourinho brings Real Madrid to the Stadio Olimpico
text: Well Tuesday's games sure didn't disappoint. Saka got his scoring boots on in a 3-0 win for Arsenal over Lille, just like we told you he would, and Barcelona once again ran up the score, so we were 2-2 on that front. Though the real drama was in Manchester United entering yet another crisis with a 2-0 loss to Atletico Madrid and Bayern Munich drawing 3-3 with the Norwegian underdogs, Viking.
As for Wednesday's game, well there's only one place to start.

Almost the last aspect of Manchester City to find itself under the microscope over recent weeks has been the team here and now under Enzo Maresca's leadership and their ability to win games in the weeks ahead. One might argue that that is a fitting aspect of the suite of punishments that will be meted out unless they are successful in their appeal. City's 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules have warped both the English and European game for so long that the temptation for some might be just not to look.

That might work in the Premier League, where the prospect of points deductions or expulsion means that games like Sunday's 3-0 win at Liverpool might actually prove to have been irrelevant. The Champions League is rather different. UEFA struck out in their probe in 2020, the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturning a two-year Champions League ban as the alleged breaches were mostly either time-barred or not established.

Whatever City achieve in Europe this season is much more likely to count. The idea of this team playing in the EFL and UCL as holders next season ought not to be entirely discounted. Most bookmakers have them as fifth or sixth favorites, at worst somewhere just outside the inner circle of contenders. Opta gives only Arsenal a better chance of winning the competition.

The current Premier League table tells you they could achieve a great deal given they have won six of six to go with their win in Porto to start off the competition. It might not be entirely truthful at this early juncture. Pep Guardiola is due to return to the Etihad on Wednesday night to offer his support to the embattled club (and, based on his public statements, the ownership too). What he will see is a team that is so far yet to kick some of the bad habits that cost them titles in his final years.

In particular, this team looks vulnerable to being cut through on the counter for reasons that will be relatively obvious if you check their pass network in last month's 5-3 win over Sunderland. Enzo Maresca's system is written as a 4-2-3-1 but Enzo Fernandez (No.17 above) is as much an attacking midfielder at the Etihad as he was when these two were together at Chelsea. The Sunderland game is an extreme example of his positioning and that of No.10 Rayan Cherki, but this bears a few hallmarks of Guardiola's time with a 4-3-3 of free eights in Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva, both superior pressers to the current attacking midfielders. It is fair to say that even a toned-down version of this approach is contingent on Elliot Anderson (No.5) continuing to be as excellent as he has been early in his City career.

Certainly it might well look vulnerable if Paris Saint-Germain show up with their midfield at full strength. The relatively diffident approach the back-to-back champions take to the league phase is a reminder not to overindex any results that don't go their way. Equally, one could see Desire Doue flitting infield and/or Ousmane Dembele dropping off the front to overwhelm Anderson and create angles for runners from wide areas.

"We need the perfect performance because they are the best team in Europe," said Maresca of the task ahead of City. "They have won the past two Champions Leagues. We need the perfect game but, doing our best, I think we can beat them and be happy at the end." Whether anyone would be happy for them is quite another matter.
Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14 | Time: 3 p.m. ETLocation: Etihad Stadium -- Manchester, United KingdomLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Man City +115; Draw +280; PSG +190

Jose Mourinho will probably relish the welcome the Stadio Olimpico affords him on his return to the side he led to the Conference League. When the ball gets rolling? Perhaps not so much. His Real Madrid side are of course favorites given the sheer weight of talent they can roll onto the field -- enough to down Inter in their Champions League opener -- but while Mourinho still puzzles out the right system to nullify the issues with the left-leaning attack, he is running into an opponent that knows exactly who they are. And Roma will be changing for no one.

"Our attitude led us to play these types of matches and finish third last year," head coach Gianpiero Gasperini said. "We have characteristics we don't change. We know Real's value, but they aren't the first valuable team we meet. It doesn't take them much to create dangerous situations, but that's part of what makes great teams great. I don't think Roma's characteristics should be distorted."

That Gasperini went on to suggest Wednesday's opponents have "room for improvement" "in terms of the aesthetic quality of their football" seemed less like a dig from a rival coach and more an expert assessment. Few coaches are as adept as Gasperini at getting their team to hum in possession, whose Roma outfit rank seventh in Europe's top five leagues in terms of non-penalty expected goals per game.

The talent is impressive but not remarkably so, the closest Roma have to a star being Paulo Dybala defying age curves in the Eternal City. Meanwhile, players have started over 30 Serie A games since the start of last season, a number that would surely be higher if Dybala were always fit. Across the pitch there are groupings that just seem to click, most notably the steadying Bryan Cristante offering a platform for Manu Kone to excel in midfield. The rich run of form that propelled this side into the Champions League at the back end of last season and the title race early in this is a triumph of the collective.

Well, that and a bit of coaching stardust. Since arriving in Italy in January, Donyell Malen has 24 Serie A goals. Across Europe's top five leagues, only five players beat that mark. The evidence of Gasperini's time at Atalanta suggests this is less a matter of Roma unlocking superstar talent, more that their coach can turn ordinary forwards into world beaters.

In a 3-5-2 system with fearless wing backs, Roma look like a team that could give Real Madrid plenty of issues in the likely event that Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Junior leave the out-of-possession stuff to the rest of their side. Now, of course, those players could puncture the bubble of their fearless hosts with just a couple of chances. Gasperini, though, has every reason to back the courage of his convictions. This is a team that could deliver quite an upset.
Date: Wednesday, Oct. 14 | Time: 3 p.m. ETLocation: Stadio Olimpico -- RomeLive stream: Paramount+Odds: Roma +250; Draw +280; Real Madrid -118

A disastrous 2025-26 season for Chelsea meant that Stamford Bridge might have stood empty for much of the winter. Happily for Shakhtar Donetsk, that is not the case, the Ukrainian champions are playing the first of their four home league phase games against AEK Athens in west London. The ties that Mykhailo Mudryk's transfer forged between the Premier League giants and Shakhtar, without a home since 2014 and unable to host European games in Ukraine since the invasion of Russia, remain strong, such that Blues owner Behdad Eghbali was only too ready to lend his stadium out.

You can read more about how Shakhtar and their ownership plan to use their London visits to draw investment in Ukraine here, but there is also the football to consider. The Ukrainian champions gave an impressive account of themselves in drawing at PSV Eindhoven in their first game, all the more so given that an XI with an average age of 24 is the youngest in the competition so far. It may be that they do not have long left with head coach Arda Turan, the subject of several links with the vacant Turkey job, and that increases the importance of this game. A win at their new home and Shakhtar would be well set for a first knockout berth since 2014-15.
