text: Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences

I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.

In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.

Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins.

As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers.

So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide.

For example, if subsidence – which is made worse by drought – damages a number of homes in your area, insurers may exclude this from your policy, so you won’t be covered if subsidence then hits your house.

When that happens to an entire community, businesses leave, investment dries up and the local economy tanks. Now imagine this happening in multiple towns around the country, at the same time. And subsidence is just one such issue, alongside wildfires, coastal erosion, wind and floods – and that’s just in the UK.

I have respect for underwriters who are just doing their jobs, and I know that no single individual is responsible. My concern lies with the attitude of much of the industry towards modellers, actuaries and researchers: there is a sense that we are an inconvenience to the deal-making process, rather than an essential part of risk management. We are the failsafe that stops our industry from reckless gambling.

At the largest scale, misquoted insurance can damage insurers, companies, their employees and the communities that rely on them. The upshot is that our customers are likely to be much more exposed to climate-related risks than they realise. People are not budgeting for a major increase in their insurance premiums or planning for their homes becoming uninsurable, but many of them absolutely should be.

If the worst happens, the insurance industry may not have the money to pay every claim when a major disaster hits. That would have profound consequences for the economy as a whole – businesses could go bankrupt, the housing market could seize up and, if people couldn’t pay their mortgages, banks would fail.
As natural catastrophes continue to become less predictable and more severe, the foundations of our entire economy will only become more fragile. Our customers deserve to know.

The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of their Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

op.title: In Germany the mood is dark. But the Weimar narrative is a far right trap | Klaus Brinkbäumer
op.desc: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end There is one experience we in Germany can all find mildly satisfying this autumn, as we watch the dark and terrifying final season of the hit TV series Babylon Berlin . We know everything those fearless (a few of them) or frightened (many more) and opportunistic (the majority) people on the screen do not. We know their future. Made by the public broadcaster ARD, Babylon Berlin has run for over 10 years, brilliantly fictionalising how Germany sleepwalked
text: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end

There is one experience we in Germany can all find mildly satisfying this autumn, as we watch the dark and terrifying final season of the hit TV series Babylon Berlin. We know everything those fearless (a few of them) or frightened (many more) and opportunistic (the majority) people on the screen do not. We know their future.

Made by the public broadcaster ARD, Babylon Berlin has run for over 10 years, brilliantly fictionalising how Germany sleepwalked into nazism and the second world war. The fifth and last season begins in January 1933 with Adolf Hitler appointed Reichskanzler.

Our funny and beautiful police detective superheroine Charlotte Ritter and the also beautiful, less funny and slightly more dubious detective Gereon Rath – both fictional – are still arguing and falling in and out of love as they chase criminals and Nazis, who are becoming synonymous. Berlin is still singing, dancing. loving. Newspapers are still being printed. Trains still run. The Jewish lawyer Hans Litten – a historical figure – still believes in German laws and German integrity (the real Litten ended up killing himself in Dachau in 1938).

Watching the show 93 years after the events being depicted, I constantly want to shout at the screen: turn left here – you can kill Hitler at this dinner, and the Reichstag won’t burn, and it will all end differently. Wake up, I want to scream at the opportunistic majority – don’t you understand what is happening?

They don’t, of course. They turn the other way and fail to kill Hitler. Because facts are facts. The dramatists are accurately describing February 1933 as the month in which German society was radically torn apart at an extraordinary speed because of mistakes made by party leaders and others who could still have stopped it all. ⁠

The timing could hardly be more apt. Babylon Berlin began streaming in 2017, the year the extreme-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) entered the Bundestag for the first time with 12.6 % of the vote. Nine years on, the AfD has become my country’s dominant political force. In September it won 44% of the vote in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the latter contest, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU dropped to 4.9% and didn’t even garner enough votes to enter the state parliament – an unprecedented humiliation.
It is, therefore, quite tempting to watch Babylon Berlin and see ourselves in those historic times. But does it make sense? It does, but not in the way you might expect.

There are not millions of desperate unemployed people on today’s German streets, nor paramilitary armies fighting heated battles. There is no Versailles trauma and the last global financial crisis was in 2008. There is no German president systematically replacing parliamentary government with emergency rule.

The German men’s football team coach, Jürgen Klopp, recently advised the nation to look at its strengths rather than constantly stare at what is not working, so let’s start there. Germany has a strong constitutional court system and powerful federal states; it has, with help from its partners, created and maintained European integration, along with an established democratic culture and institutions designed explicitly because of the lessons of Weimar. Our European Germany in 2026 is not Weimar Germany in 1933.

But there is another connection between Babylon Berlin and us as German spectators today – an echo that is more subtle and more interesting. It lies in this conviction that everything is falling apart. Here the wonderfully tongue-breaking term selbsterfüllende Prophezeiung (self-fulfilling prophecy) comes into play.

Germany excels at the one thing no country should aspire to be good at. We are constantly describing ourselves as a country in terminal decline. Just spend an evening watching political talkshows or listening to people around you, and you will conclude that we are witnessing the final collapse of a failed state.

The trains are all late. Bridges and streets are crumbling. Schools are failing and German children lagging behind in Pisa rankings. Bureaucracy is suffocating business and taxes are sky-high, plus ineffectively used. Isn’t energy too expensive and our pension system unsustainable? Immigration is out of control. Our digital transformation is a joke. And as for our car industry, that is on its knees. Plus, we lost to Ecuador and Paraguay at the World Cup. And the government cannot agree on how to fix any of this because support for the two big mainstream parties (the centre-right CDU and the centre-left SPD) is shrinking, and coalitions between parties that hate each other have become ever more complicated and fragile.

I started writing these lines on a train from Hamburg to Tübingen via Stuttgart which was delayed by two hours. Someone in the hierarchy of Deutsche Bahn (or an AI, of course) then decided that, as we were already this late, the train would terminate in Mannheim. I had to cancel my plans and instead turn around and go back home. This is how you spend a day in modern Germany.

Something much larger than my individual problem has arisen, however: our national narrative of failure has developed a disturbing relationship with reality. Germany’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed back above 3 million in September and inflation reached 3.3%.

Within the world of public broadcasting, talk about reform has been imminent for more than a decade – but instead of building the strongest and most robust system possible, which then might actually withstand the shocks, there are simply more meetings, and more reports, and more commissions of inquiry.

The biggest problem, though, is Germany’s belief in the enormity of its problems. And this is exactly where Babylon Berlin and its look at 1933 becomes a more relevant companion to 2026 than the “Weimar is back” cry suggests .

Democracies become vulnerable when people cease to believe that democracy can deliver. The destruction of Weimar was preceded by such a loss of faith. The circumstances were and are fundamentally different now. But one political mechanism is recognisable: the extreme right has a brief and simple story to tell.
Close the borders. Deport those people we don’t know. Ignore Brussels. Stop paying Ukraine. Bring back cheap Russian energy and abolish stupid climate rules. Put Germany first.

Our society seems scared and exhausted from years of crisis after crisis, and from the alarming talk of never-ending crises of tomorrow. The AfD understands this and knows how to turn every minor and unresolved problem into evidence that “das System” is rotten. My cancelled train is no longer just that, but proof of national doom. The brilliance of declinism lies in the fact that it is self-confirming. Once you have accepted that the country is collapsing, you see nothing but evidence for it.
Would we recognise the end of our democracy if it were happening today, and to us? Or, instead, would we recognise the strength of our democracy if it were not ending?

There is a danger in catastrophising so much that we cease to notice resilience, and progress, and that many things work just fine. German angst becomes German cynicism; cynicism turns to contempt; and, finally, contempt will make the AfD’s promise of destruction sound like the renewal we all need.

We can and must tell the other, true story, of a country that has found trusted friends and partners and hence a peace that has lasted for 80 years, and economic and political, cultural and scientific successes most nations dream of – even in football (although it has become increasingly difficult to remember those days).

This is not 1933 revisited, but it is a serious moment. And a good moment to for a reminder that, in dangerous times, a democratic coalition needs to govern as decisively, effectively and empathetically as it possibly can.
Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is a podcast and TV host in Germany and has published nine books

news.title: Man, 62, dies after torrential floods sweep car onto beach on Greek island of Rhodes
news.desc: A 62-year-old hotel employee died on the Greek island of Rhodes after his car was swept onto a beach by floodwaters as a severe storm battered parts of the country
text: A car swept away by floodwaters in Stegna, Rhodes(Image: Eurokinissi/AFP via Getty Images)
A 62-year-old man has died after his car was swept onto a beach by torrential floodwaters on the Greek island of Rhodes.
The incident happened in Stegna, around 20 miles south of Rhodes Town, early on Wednesday afternoon, as a severe storm battered parts of Greece.

The island was hit by exceptionally heavy rainfall, with Greece’s public broadcaster ERT reporting that more than 200mm of rain fell in six and a half hours. The Greek fire service said emergency crews received 113 calls on Rhodes by 4pm local time, carrying out 64 water-pumping operations and evacuating 13 people to safety.
The man, who worked at a local hotel, had attempted to retrieve his car it was swept by torrents of water, according to residents who spoke to the MEGA TV channel.

His body was later found among reeds and debris on the beach, according to ERT. The Greek coast guard confirmed that a man had been found unconscious in the waters off Stegna, where it said four cars had been swept away by the floodwaters.

Several major tourist attractions on the island were closed from 12.30pm local time as a precaution to protect visitors and staff. They included the archaeological sites of Lindos, Kamiros and the Acropolis of Ialysos-Filerimos, as well as the Archaeological Museum of Rhodes and the Palace of the Grand Master, according to Greek news outlet Protothema.

The severe weather also caused widespread flooding and disruption in other parts of Greece. Evia, a large island north-east of Athens, was among the areas most severely affected, with torrential rain causing rivers to overflow, flooding communities and damaging roads.
A man attempts to cross a flooded road in Rhodes(Image: LEFTERIS DAMIANIDIS/EPA/Shutterstock)
Flooding and disruption were also reported on the Sporades islands, including Skiathos and Skopelos, as well as in parts of the Attica region, including central Athens.

According to ERT, rainfall totals reached around 310mm in Evia, 280mm in Rhodes, 258mm on Skopelos and 173mm in Attica's Agia Triada within just a few hours. Meanwhile, around 29,000 lightning strikes were recorded across the Aegean.
Conditions are expected to improve gradually before further rain and thunderstorms hit eastern Thessaly, the Sporades, Evia and Central Greece from Friday evening into Saturday afternoon.

news.title: Boy, 9, who died with parents and brother in Waterford fire had heart surgery just weeks ago
news.desc: Jayden English, nine, who died following an arson attack on his home in County Waterford, Ireland, had undergone heart surgery just two weeks prior
text: A nine-year-old boy who died along with his parents and older brother following a suspected arson attack at their home in Ireland had undergone heart surgery just two weeks earlier, it has been revealed.
Jayden, nine, his brother Callum, 12, and their parents, Philip and Kim English, all died in the fire at their home on Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford, in the early hours of Tuesday.
The couple’s two other children, a 14-year-old girl and a six-year-old boy, remained in a critical condition in hospital on Wednesday, the Irish Mirror reports.

Jayden and Callum were both born with heart defects, according to a social media post shared in 2020 by BUMBLEance, Ireland's children's ambulance service. Jayden had undergone a heart surgery just two weeks before the tragedy, Irish public broadcaster RTÉ reported.
In a tribute posted on social media on Wednesday afternoon, the ambulance service remembered the two boys and their parents for touching "the hearts of many during their time travelling with us".
"We will always cherish the memories we have and remember the times we shared on board. Our team are without words as we try to process this unimaginable loss," the tribute read.
"We extend our deepest condolences to their family during this devastating time and our thoughts & prayers to their siblings in critical condition.
"Please know that you are not alone in your grief; the whole community stands beside you, offering love and support during these difficult days ahead."
Jayden's brother Callum also lost his life in the blaze(Image: @Johnville Fc/Facebook)
At a prayer vigil at Sacred Heart Church on Wednesday evening, Father Gerry Chestnutt called on the local community to "wrap each other in love".
"We may even find words hard to speak, but our emotions can be shown," he told the congregation of around 500.

"Each one of us knows that what happened in Birch Avenue yesterday should never, ever have happened. An innocent family preparing for a new day should have done what they did every day: parents preparing their children for school.

"An innocent family taken from our midst in a most horrific and violent way. I want to say, even though they're not here, that the persons responsible need to have the courage now to stand up, admit what you did and face the legal consequences of what you did.
"And I would also say to all here present: if you know anything whatsoever about what happened on Birch Avenue, please contact An Garda Síochána."

news.title: World's oldest shipwreck - thought to be 4,700 years old - found off coast of Turkey
news.desc: The shipwreck dates back to the Early Bronze Age and is believed to have been built around the same time as the Great Pyramid of Giza
text: Archaeologists with artefacts from the shipwreck(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)
The world's oldest-known shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, which archaeologists have dated back 4,400 to 4,700 years ago.

The ship was dated back to the Early Bronze Age and is believed to have been built around the same time as the construction of the Great Pyramid. Researchers said they believe the wreck could have been a trade vessel that was carrying goods across the Mediterranean Sea. The wooden structure of the ship had not survived but ceramic pots carried on the ship were remarkably discovered on the sea floor.
Some of these pots incredibly even included traces of what they held inside thousands of years ago.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.
The pots were recovered by divers(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The wreck was discovered off the coast of Kekova Island, in Antalya, southern Turkey. The ship was around 10m long, according to the researchers from Mediterranean Archaeology Association who made the discovery.
Archaeologists said they fond artefacts on an underwater slope, 30m deep into the sea. Some of the items retrieved included 30 ceramic pots and three large stone anchors.
The discovery was made near the coast of Kekova Island, by Antalya(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)
Despite the wooden structure of the ship not surviving, archaeologists were able to date the discovery to 2600-2400 BC, making it the oldest discovered shipwreck in the world.

A study of the discovery, in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology, said: "Current information suggests that the shipwreck is from a small vessel that sank while sailing east to west during the Early Bronze Age."

Researchers dated wreck by analysing the shape of the ceramic pots, called amphorae, as different styles link to different periods of time. These pots had two handles on either side, a flat base and ridge in the middle.
A shipwreck believed to be up to 4,700 years old was discovered(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

The expedition was led by Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, and he said that matched the pottery styles from the Early Bronze Age popular in the Levant - modern-day Syria, Lebanon Palestine and Israel.
Prof Öniz said: "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%" He added: "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea."

The pots were brought out of the water by divers and the artefacts are now being conserved by experts. Archaeologist Dr Karin Sowada, from Macquarie University, Australia, looked the amphorae after they were recovered.

Dr Sowada said she was shocked to see the pots still contained a viscous, glossy residue, according to the BBC. She said: "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining."
Experts are now examining what the pots could have been used for as Dr Sowada suggested they could have carried wine, olive oil or tree resins.

She added: "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."

news.title: Six dead, including child, in horror Wisconsin plane crash as aircraft plunges into woods
news.desc: Six people - including a child - were killed after a small plane crashed in rural Wisconsin on Tuesday night
text: Five adults and one child were on board the plane(Image: FOX6 News Milwaukee)
Six people - including a child - have died in a small plane crash in rural Wisconsin.
The fixed-wing Piper went down at around 9.30pm CDT on Tuesday (3.30am BST on Wednesday) in the town of Dellona, about 125 miles from Milwaukee, the Sauk County Sheriff’s Office said.

Five adults and one child were on board the plane, which was returning from Kenosha to Menomonie, Wisconsin, officials said. According to FlightAware, the plane left Kenosha Regional Airport shortly before 9pm CDT.
The plane was found in a "densely wooded area", where "all six occupants of the aircraft were located deceased on scene", the sheriff's office said.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the aircraft was a Piper PA-46.
There were no reports of damage to structures or injuries to people on the ground, according to the sheriff's office.
Investigators are working "to determine the circumstances surrounding the crash", the sheriff's office said.
The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are investigating the crash, with the NTSB leading the investigation, said the FAA.

news.title: Student, 23, sentenced to death over social media post that 'insulted' prophet
news.desc: Accounting student Najmeh Amini, 23, is to be executed for blasphemy after she was involved in anti-regime protests earlier in the year
text: Iranian student Najmeh Amini, 23 was sentenced to death last month
A 23-year-old woman has been sentenced to death in Iran after making a social media post that authorities say insulted the prophet.
Accounting student Najmeh Amini, 23, was sentenced to death for blasphemy last month after she had spent eight months in the notorious Vakilabad Prison in Mashhad.
The regime previously said it was holding her on charges including “'insulting the Supreme Leader” and “clashing with security agents”.
It has now been revealed by Iranian human rights activists that she was in fact sentenced to death on charges of 'sab ol-nabi' (insulting the prophet).
She was also given a prison sentence of 12 years, six months, and one day for the charges of acting against national security and spreading anti-regime propaganda.
Earlier this year Amini took part in a mass street protest against the authoritarian Iranian government and it was here that she was arrested on January 31.
The regime's brutal crackdown following the protests saw more than 7,000 people killed, and thousands more were arrested, human rights groups have said.
In a leaked audio recording from inside the jail last month Amini can be heard desperately pleading for help following her sentencing.
“Greetings to the people of Iran. I am Najmeh Amini, 23 years old, speaking from the central prison of Mashhad. I am leaving this message for you on 18 September 2026,” she says on the recording.

“I am not trying to make a hero out of myself today; I only ask one thing: be my voice. I am an innocent girl, a young person with so many hopes and dreams. I have parents who are waiting for me— a family that wakes up every morning fearing my loss.
“I do not want the last remaining trace of me to be a few lines in a case file.
“If my voice reaches outside the prison, please do not listen to it for just a moment and then forget it!

“People, I only want justice and the opportunity to defend myself. I request that lawyers, legal scholars, human rights activists, and everyone who hears the voices of innocent people review my case file.
“I request that international human rights organisations and responsible bodies at the United Nations hear my voice and investigate and follow up on the status of my case.
“Remember my name; I may not be able to speak again. But as long as I am alive, I hold one hope: that before the rope marks the end of my life, I see my prosperous and free Iran,' she added.”
Tehran regularly executes political prisoners, often at public hangings.

Iran Human Rights Monitor said: “Issuing a death sentence against a 23-year-old student after months of arbitrary detention, reported risk of torture, and complete denial of counsel doubles the urgency for immediate international intervention to stay and overturn this sentence.”

Heba Morayef, Amnesty International's regional director recently said: “The Iranian authorities are unleashing a horrifying wave of executions and death sentences to punish and suppress dissent and project an image of strength and absolute control”.
“The muted response from the international community emboldens the Iranian authorities to continue their deadly rampage.”
At least 26 people have been executed for offences related to the January protests and at least 60 others, including three arrested as children, remain at risk of execution, Amnesty said.

news.title: Massive explosion at factory in Israel with casualties reported amid 'stay away' warning
news.desc: At least three people have been seriously injured in an explosion at a factory in Kiryat Gat, southern Israel
text: The explosion left the factory in Israel burning(Image: Israel Fire and Rescue Authority)
Several people have been badly injured in a huge explosion and fire at a factory in Israel with hazardous chemicals feared to have leaked from the site.
A spokesperson for Israeli medical emergency service United Hatzalah said three people had suffered burns across their body following the blast.

Israel's Fire and Rescue Authority also reported that hazardous chemicals had possibly leaked as a result of the explosion, and that they were currently working to locate the source of the chemicals, as well as extinguish the fire, the Jerusalem Post reports. Police and emergency rescue services have warned people to stay away.

Israel Police said that the explosion was suspected to have been caused by the detonation of a gas cylinder. The police also confirmed that the explosion had not been caused by hostile terrorist activity.

Yanaki Weinberg, deputy head of United Hatzalah’s Kiryat Gat branch, and paramedic Moshe Winfeld said they treated a man aged around 45 who was critically injured and suffered burns across his body. He was transported by ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway. The team delivered two electric shocks using a defibrillator and the man's heart began beating again, they said.
Intel’s Kiryat Gat factory manufactures semiconductor chips and is also known as FAB 28.

news.title: Inside the smart fridges and freezers targeted by hackers in French cyberattack as experts issue warning
news.desc: A massive cyberattack hit thousands of fridge and freezer units across Europe this week, leading to warnings about potential vulnerabilities in the software that runs them
text: Supermarkets were hit across Europe in the massive attack(Image: AP Photo/Teresa Suarez)
A cyber attack targeting supermarket fridges across Europe that caused millions of Euros in damages should "raise alarm bells" for Britain, experts have warned.

The attack saw hundreds of supermarkets, primarily in France, left without functional units after hackers gained entry to their software and turned up the temperature. Some warmed to temperatures of 50C overnight, according to the chief executive of Coopérative U, one supermarket chain that was affected by the mass breach.

Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also among those hit in the attack, which also hit Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium but to a lesser extent - and experts believe the UK could be next.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.
The hack targeted systems made by different manufacturers(Image: AP Photo/Teresa Suarez)
Modern supermarkets use a combination of different fridge and freezer systems, including multideck open chillers, glass-doored display cabinets, and the large chest freezers.

These are industrial setups which are not available commercially, and they run on digital systems connected to a single localised network. This means it is possible for bad actors with the right software to gain entry and control the settings these networks govern.
When they do so, the hackers can control the temperature of each fridge unit, activate their defrost cycles, and any remote energy usage.
Customers were warned about the impact of the hack in pinned notices(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)
In the case of this week's cyberattack, hackers gained access to specific remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss, US-based Copeland and Dixell.

Danfoss said on Monday that hackers were able to gain entry to the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 products, which, it added, no longer received software or security updates. The firm added that it was working with affected customers to limit the damage.

The company said in a statement: "We are working with affected customers to implement appropriate mitigation measures, including firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable."
A spokesperson for Copeland, which owns Dixell, said the firm's top priority is protecting the operations of its customers.
The hack may have caused millions in lost revenue, it is believed(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)
According to French outlet BFM-TV, hackers forced a continuous defrost cycle and set temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F) on stores’ refrigeration systems.

No one has claimed responsibility for the hack just yet, and CERT-FR, France's national computer emergency response team, said earlier this week that it was unclear how the hackers gained access to the system. The agency also did not outline a specific vulnerability, firmware version, or way in the attackers may have used.
Instead, it issued an alert to supermarkets using the affected systems warning them against exposing management interfaces to the internet.

The spokesperson said it had identified a "vulnerability" in a "discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers", adding it would be working to mitigate the risks posed by the hack. They said: "We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk."
It was primarily French supermarkets that were affected by the hack(Image: AP Photo/Bob Edme)
British supermarkets use the same technology to cool and freeze products, but they don't use Danfoss units quite as widely as their French counterparts.

The UK has a host of its own firms that manufacture fridge and freezer units, including Arneg UK, AHT Cooling Systems UK and Hussmann UK, which are used across a wide variety of different supermarkets. They are still present, however, according to cyber defence agency UK Cyber Defence.

The firm told The Grocer it found 15 Danfoss fridges across the country that were accessible on the open internet. The firm said it was "accurate to say it is highly unlikely that they have been patched".
Experts have said the hackers could target similar vulnerabilities in British supermarket fridge units(Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)
Speaking to The Mirror, Simon Michie, Managing Director at Risk Crew, said the principles deployed in hacking could also transfer to other vendors in future cyber attacks.

He said: “While the situation is developing and we don’t know the root cause yet, the security weaknesses are familiar from other technology environments. Attackers appear to have exploited outdated equipment that had reached its end of life, with no recent security updates available.
"In this case, it’s likely the equipment was reachable by the hackers because the store’s operational technology network is joined to the business network.

"The risk could have been reduced by disconnecting the outdated equipment from the network, preventing attackers from accessing it remotely, which has clearly not happened. There is also a chance this was a supply chain attack via the Danfoss software monitoring service.

"Of course, the principles transfer to other OT (operational technology) vendors. The lesson is to pay more attention to OT networks and connected devices, which are often off the radar, such as copiers, webcams and other appliance."
The attacks 'should ring alarm bells' in the UK, an expert has warned(Image: AFP via Getty Images)
Marijus Briedis, Chief Technology Officer at NordVPN, said the attacks "should ring alarm bells" in Britain, especially if retailers are using internet-connected systems.

He said: “The cyberattack on supermarket fridges in France should ring alarm bells in Britain. If UK retailers use internet-connected refrigeration systems with similar security weaknesses, hackers could cause the same disruption here.
"There is no evidence British supermarkets have been affected by this incident, but distance offers little protection when criminals can reach vulnerable equipment remotely.

“Hackers don't need to get into the tills to cause havoc in a supermarket. Interfere with the equipment keeping food cold and you can force stores to throw away valuable stock, shut entire aisles and leave shoppers facing empty fridges and freezers.

"A cyberattack can quickly become a food safety problem, as well as a very expensive one for retailers. British supermarkets should be checking their connected refrigeration systems now, especially older equipment that may no longer receive security updates.

"Remote access needs to be tightly controlled, critical systems separated from the wider network and independent temperature alerts and manual checks in place. One vulnerable controller should not be allowed to put an entire store's chilled food at risk.”

news.title: Pope Leo lung surgery: Vatican issues update after pontiff's cancer diagnosis
news.desc: Pope Leo XIV has undergone a 90-minute operation at the Policlinico A. Gemelli hospital in Rome which saw surgeons remove the lower lobe of the 71-year-old’s right lung after finding a cancerous nodule
text: Pope Leo XIV has spent a peaceful night in hospital after an operation following his diagnosis with lung cancer, the Vatican has said.
The diagnosis came after an operation which saw doctors remove a growth from the 71-year-old’s right lung.
An examination of the nodule during the operation led doctors to confirm that the religious leader had adenocarcinoma.
"The surgery was successful, and there were no further complications, the statement said. The Vatican said there were currently no plans for the Pope to begin chemotherapy or other therapies.

Messages of support and well wishes have flooded in after the surgery, which was performed at a hospital in Rome, the Policlinico A. Gemelli. The Vatican previously said Leo will spend about a week in hospital recovering from the operation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is among those who have taken to X to offer his best wishes.
In a brief message posted to X, Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrote: “From the holy city of Jerusalem, I wish Pope Leo XIV a full and speedy recovery.”
Maltese Prime Minister Robert Abela also extended “prayers and best wishes” to the pope for “a successful procedure and a complete recovery.”

Pope Leo also received prayers from Anglican Archbishop Sarah Mullaly of Canterbury, who said she was “holding Pope Leo XIV in my prayers over these coming days, asking for God’s protection, closeness and care.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took to X to send well wishes to the pope, he wished Pope Leo “a successful surgery and a swift, full recovery.”

“Our thoughts and prayers are with him, and we hope he will soon be back in good health and strength,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Ukraine is deeply grateful to His Holiness for his prayers and his strong, consistent calls for a dignified and durable peace.”
(Image: Ukrainian Presidency Press Offic/ZUMA Press Wire Service/REX/Shutterstock)
Italian President Sergio Mattarella published a letter to Pope Leo saying that the news of his surgery “was received with deep empathy and emotion by all the Italian people.”

“In view of your hospitalization in the coming days, may the affectionate thoughts of all Italians reach you, which I convey while adding my own personal sentiments,” Mattarella wrote. “The Italian people stand close to you.”

The Italian head of state said the pope could count on the prayers of not only the Catholic faithful, but also “on the caring thoughts of countless people, in Italy as well as across the world, whether believers or non-believers.”
Sergio Mattarella, President of the Italian Republic(Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The Holy See Press Office says Pope Leo XIV had a calm first night in Rome's Gemelli Hospital.

"The night passed calmly for the Pope. Further information will be provided later today," the Holy See Press Office said on Wednesday, the morning after Pope Leo underwent a successful lung operation with no complications.
During his Sunday noon prayer, Leo revealed doctors had discovered a small nodule on his lung, adding that he would have it removed.
Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, developing in cells that produce mucus, usually in the outer parts of the lungs.
It is a form of non-small cell lung cancer, and treatment depends on factors including how far the cancer has spread.
Oncologists previously said that even if the growth proved to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis was "excellent" as the nodule was removed at an early stage.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo said that the pope had said he felt "nothing wrong" physically during a meeting on Monday.
He said Leo had chosen to check in for surgery as soon as possible due to a scheduled trip to Latin America in early November which he was keen not to miss.

Churches across the world prayed for the pope yesterday as he underwent the surgery. An evening rosary that was held in the chapel of the hospital, presided over by Cardinal Baldassarre Reina, papal vicar of Rome.
Churches and religious communities across Rome were also invited to pray the rosary, Vatican Radio reported.

Vatican News reported that churches in several countries are celebrating Mass, including the pope's hometown of Chicago at St. Mary of the Angels Church and Chiclayo, and his former diocese in Chiclayo, Peru, where its cathedral held a Mass for him.
Pope Leo XIV greets people as he arrives at hospital(Image: Maria Laura Antonelli/AGF/Shutterstock)

Archbishop Richard Moth, Archbishop of Westminster and President of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales, said on Sunday that he had sent a message to the 71-year-old American pontiff as he prepared for his surgery.
He said: “We pray that following the procedure and a period of recovery, he will soon be restored to health.
“I have sent a message on behalf of all in the Catholic Church in England and Wales, assuring him of our prayers.”
Dr Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora issued the following statement yesterday following the pope's operation:

"To ensure a radical procedure, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique. The intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected by the pre-operative tests.
"The Holy Father was in the operating theatre for approximately three hours; the operation itself lasted about ninety minutes. The operation was successful and there were no complications.
"Following the operation, the Pope woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor.
"The surgical team was led by Professor Stefano Margaritora, assisted by Professor Elisa Meacci, Dr Maria Teresa Congedo and Dr Leonardo Petracca Caravella.
"The anaesthesia team consisted of Professor Massimo Antonelli, Dr Giovanni Punzo and Dr Giuseppe Bello."
