Mayor Thodoris Tzoumas revealed that up to 50 businesses and 20 homes had suffered damage as power cuts plunged parts of the island into darkness.
He said: “The rain and winds continue. We are carrying out repairs to the main network, where we have some power outages.
“We had some trees fall and two cars have been swept away, while schools are closed. The phenomenon seems to be subsiding.”
Meanwhile, residents in Evia were ordered to flee towards Psachna after the Kireas River burst its banks, severing a major road connection.
Emergency alerts also urged people across the island to avoid unnecessary journeys as the deluge continued.
In another dramatic incident, two people were rescued after their sailing boat ran aground near the island of Peristera amid powerful winds.
Greece’s Civil Protection Ministry warned that dangerous conditions could persist into Wednesday evening, with further heavy downpours and violent gusts forecast.
The deadly storm comes just weeks after devastating floods tore through Crete, destroying infrastructure, crops and livestock.
A 79-year-old shepherd was found dead on the island during the earlier weather disaster.

news.title: Fears US has cut off intel to Ukraine leaving country wide open to Putin’s deadly blitzes after Musk ‘limits Starlink’
news.desc: FEARS are mounting the US has stopped sending vital intelligence to Ukraine after its military suffered a sudden Starlink outage. Donald Trump is continuing to pile pressure on Volodymyr Zelensky to stop Kyiv's strikes on the Russian oil industry. Ukrainian military missions were abandoned up by the abrupt outage of Elon Musk's satellite-based internet service,...
text: FEARS are mounting the US has stopped sending vital intelligence to Ukraine after its military suffered a sudden Starlink outage.
Donald Trump is continuing to pile pressure on Volodymyr Zelensky to stop Kyiv’s strikes on the Russian oil industry.
Ukrainian military missions were abandoned up by the abrupt outage of Elon Musk‘s satellite-based internet service, Zelensky’s advisers said.
Musk’s SpaceX, which owns and operates Starlink services, has put a 100mph “speed limit” on the Starshield military package of satellite devices without warning, Kyiv officials said.
You'll now receive top stories, breaking news, and more, straight to your email.
They added that the restrictions were limiting Ukraine’s mid-range and long-range strikes against Russia.
Later Ukrainian units said the speed limit dropped even further to 40mph.
Trump threatens to cut off vital US weapons to Ukraine in row with Zelensky
Trump calls for Zelensky to be replaced as he 'wants to make problems for world'
Serhii Breskrestnov, an aide to President Zelensky said: “Starlink isused to protect our skies from jet-powered Shaheds.”
He added: “By taking these steps, our partners are depriving us of oneof the few options we have for defending the country againstjet-powered Shaheds.”
Musk responded on X, writing: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus.”
Parents arrested after 9 siblings 'placed in cages' found in 'appalling' home
US choppers blow up spy boat after mine sinks container ship carrying iPhones
Pope's brother - who also has cancer - says Leo's disease 'caught early'
‘He treated me like an animal’…Every claim made by 6 women at Brand 'rape' trial
It comes after Trump told Zelensky to scrap his strikes on Russia‘s oil industry at the weekend.
Musk joined in and claimed Ukrainian bomb blitzes on Putin’s petrol producers had gone too far.

Zelensky suggested that intelligence was continuing to flow, but said in an NPR interview that his advisers had been threatened that US information sharing could be limited if they don’t stop their strikes.
Ukrainian air force spokesperson Col Yurii Ihnat said the military did not get any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening.
But he said Ukraine did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about the three barrages of missiles that followed.
SpaceX has not confirmed the changes to Starlink’s military infrastructure.
Ukrainian military radio technology specialist Serhiy Beskrestnov said super fast Starlink terminals and those on military-specific programs had suddenly been cut off.
He said: “Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions.
“It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
There are no reports that static Starlinks, which are essential for Ukrainian soldiers’ battlefield communication, have been cut off.
Musk cutting off a huge swathe of Starlink’s services for Russian soldiers helped Ukraine to make massive gains earlier this year.
The most recent SpaceX intervention comes after Trump said “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president” and claimed Zelensky wants “to make problems for the world”.
And the US president has threatened to suspend a deal letting allies buy US arms to send to Ukraine.
Trump struck a huge diesel deal with Mad Vlad on Friday to allow Russian oil to be sold to the US and the world.
Sale of sanctioned oil is a significant source of funding for the Russian tyrant’s bloodthirsty war on Ukraine.
But Trump said on Saturday that Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal” and told Zelensky to stop striking Russian oil.
The US president added: “We said, ‘you can do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries’, because that’s a world problem that’s caused.”

news.title: Seven attempts to get home, but Venezuela’s Nobel peace prize laureate is still being blocked Thomas Graham María Corina Machado hoped to return to her country after its dictator was deposed. Bizarre circumstances keep preventing her
text: Trump’s midterm meddling means a constitutional crisis is brewing
As the aircraft descended towards Caracas, Claudia Macero, one of Venezuela’s exiled opposition activists, was fretting about what the authorities might ask her.

She had fled her homeland covertly in 2025, having spent almost a year trapped in the Argentinian embassy: Venezuela’s top prosecutor had ordered her arrest for alleged treason and conspiracy against the regime of Nicolás Maduro, the country’s authoritarian leader. She didn’t even have an exit stamp in her passport and, as far as she knew, the case against her was still open.
“I didn’t have any security with me and I hadn’t let them know I was coming,” she says. “I just bought a ticket and told my lawyer what I wanted to do.”
But at the airport, to her surprise, nobody asked her anything. “Honestly, it was crazy,” she says of the feeling of relief.

“Every time [someone returns to Venezuela] it feels like it opens the space of freedom a little more, that people can feel a little more optimistic… that this is our country and we have the right to come back.”
Claudia Macero is welcomed back to Caracas at the headquarters of Vente Venezuela, the party led by Nobel laureate Maria Corina Machado

Macero is one of many exiles who have returned home to help Venezuela’s transformation, triggered in January when Donald Trump’s administration seized Maduro and rendered him to the US. At a stroke, the fear that had suffocated the political opposition for years was lifted.
But one person, arguably the most important, remains conspicuously excluded: the opposition leader and Nobel peace prizewinner, María Corina Machado.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, has said that Machado, who currently lives in Panama, can return to Venezuela whenever she wants. But after a string of attempts by land, sea and air have been thwarted in bizarre circumstances over recent months, her supporters suspect otherwise. Machado, 59, remains sidelined from a political transition that, in their eyes, she should be leading.
Trump’s midterm meddling means a constitutional crisis is brewing

“We need a leader with true legitimacy,” said Jesús Armas, an activist from Vente Venezuela, Machado’s political party, and a former political prisoner released in February. “We need María Corina Machado to come back.”

When US special forces seized Maduro and his wife from their Caracas compound on 3 January, Machado was out of the country – she had been in hiding since the 2024 elections, after which the president set out to crush the opposition and cling to power. Machado had been awarded the Nobel a month before Trump’s raid, for her efforts to promote the democratic rights of Venezuelans. Her work proved that Maduro had lost by a landslide in 2024.
When news broke that the former despot was being flown to the US to face drugs and weapons charges in New York, Machado no doubt thought her time had come.
Nicolas Maduro is seen in handcuffs after landing at a Manhattan helipad, escorted by heavily armed Federal agents

But rather than root out the old regime, Trump promoted Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s deputy.. From the outset, the new president has understood – and Trump has made clear – that her political survival depends on her willingness to obey orders from Washington.
The Trump administration then set out its three-step plan for Venezuela: stability, economic recovery and only then a political transition and new elections.

Almost a year later, Trump has boasted of securing a “historic” deal to take control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves and is eyeing its gold and mineral wealth. Oil and gas executives have flocked back to the country, hoping to make a fortune. Yet there is still no date for elections.

Machado has strived to curry favour with Trump, presenting him with her Nobel peace prize and praising the prosecution of Maduro, and has claimed she can help bring home the 8 million Venezuelans who fled the country’s economic collapse in recent years.

Despite those offerings, the Trump administration has conspicuously avoided publicly backing her return. Machado has now made seven attempts to enter Venezuela, according to her team, and each has failed.

The first time she took a private jet from Virginia, but was ordered to turn back mid-flight. On the second attempt, an airline refused to let her board a commercial flight from Panama. Her team has shared few details about the third and fourth attempts, except to say that one was by land, in case they use the same routes again in the future.

The latest three attempts took place in the space of 24 hours last month, while Rodríguez was at the UN general assembly, posing for photos with Trump and giving the peace sign. A boat journey was cancelled because of an apparent engine fault, and then two requests to land private jets on Aruba and Curaçao, the Dutch Caribbean islands off the coast of Venezuela, were rejected.
Macero, who is the communications co-ordinator for Vente, says it is Rodríguez who is blocking Machado’s return. But others see the hand of the US behind Machado’s aborted homecomings.
“People ask me about the United States, but it is neither public nor documented that there is a direct impediment,” said Macero.
She points to Rubio’s recent denial that the US was involved. “We hold on to that,” Macero says. “But obviously we understand that there are forces that do not want her to come.”
María Corina Machado speaks during a gathering of Venezuelans in Panama on May 23, 2026

What is clear is that the US is anxious to maintain stability in Venezuela. There is widespread popular discontent with Rodríguez’s government, but the regime has long kept control through an array of armed groups, from the army and police to paramilitary biker gangs.
Trump himself has pointed to the lessons of Iraq, when the decision to dismiss Saddam Hussein’s entire regime and security apparatus triggered a collapse into bloody civil war.

“When President Bush knocked out Iraq, everybody got fired. There was nobody to run it,” he told Time earlier this month. “I did the opposite. I didn’t fire the police. I didn’t fire the armies… And Delcy [Rodríguez] was the one that was in charge of things.”

Economic interests underpin the White House’s desire for stability. While US-directed negotiations between Rodríguez’s government and opposition parties – excluding Machado – have made cautious progress, economic reforms have raced ahead.

At Trump’s direction, Rodríguez has opened Venezuela’s oil and mineral reserves to foreign investment. The Pentagon itself took a stake in one private Venezuelan oil company that secured access to 17 oilfields holding 65bn barrels of oil.

“To me, the only reasonable analysis of the situation is that [the White House] believes Machado’s return would somehow upset a very fragile equilibrium that has been created for the economic opening in oil and gas and mining,” says James Story, a former US ambassador to Venezuela.
“But until we have a mass reform of all of the institutions and there’s an election, what we have is just a more profitable dictatorship.”
Machado’s team argues that her return and a firm date for new elections would bring stability and long-term investment as the government and the US commit to a democratic transition.

“I’m not so worried about the plan itself as the timeline,” said Armas. “What worries me is that Delcy is negotiating to win time. And the only thing that can control [her government] is the threat of the use of force. That’s why we need this process to advance as quickly as possible, because this was the [US] administration that dared to do something like January 3.”
Machado pressed her case again last week, writing in the New York Post that her return was “urgent”.

“I’ll say one thing: she is an excellent woman,” the president said. “She gave me her Nobel prize because she knew I had earned it, and she is an excellent woman, and everything is going to turn out fine.”
Photographs by Enea Lebrun/Getty Images, Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty Images, XNY/Star Max/GC Images

news.title: Cybercrime Barney Macintyre French supermarket fridge hackers may be shopping for kudos Young men seeking approval from their peers may be responsible for the widespread attacks
text: ‘After any woman falls to her death, police should think: domestic abuse’
Imagine reaching into a freezer at your local Intermarché only to find that the frog legs you planned to serve for dinner had been lightly broiled in their packet. Quel cauchemar!

That was the situation facing French shoppers on Monday morning after hackers found a way to raise the temperature of refrigerators and freezers ​at hundreds of retailers across the country – in some cases by up to 50C – leading to several fires and millions of euros of spoiled food.

More than 300 sites owned by French supermarkets Intermarché, Monoprix, Carrefour and E Leclerc were hit due to their dependence on software that allows cold units to be managed remotely. The software was provided by Danish company Danfoss. Fridges in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium were also affected.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK National Cyber Security Centre, has described the attack as “one of the oddest cyber events” he has ever seen. No criminal group or state-affiliated actor has yet claimed responsibility, but a similar type of attack appears to have affected commissary freezers at six US military facilities in August.

“No one’s really claimed anything, which is odd,” said Aiden Sinnott, cybersecurity researcher at Sophos. “They haven’t stolen any data. There’s nothing they can really hold to ransom here. Often state-sponsored actors are quiet, but that’s usually because one of the main purposes is espionage… whereas a disruptive attack like this is pretty noisy.”

Could it be that these hackers weren’t interested in sabotage or financial reward, but instead were seeking approval from their peers? In recent months intelligence firms have noted the rise of a new class of hacker: young, western, predominantly male groups armed with AI, who have been behind several high-profile retail hacks including the £300m shutdown of M&S last year.

Kudos for carrying out high-profile disruption is shared within online communities. The largest of these is known as “the Com”, which the FBI said “has expanded to include thousands of people”, mostly English-speaking, aged 11 to 25.
Sinnott notes that one hacker group has even set up an “in the press” section on its leak website – a kind of twisted testimonials page valorising the hackers’ ability to wreak havoc.
‘After any woman falls to her death, police should think: domestic abuse’

He also suggests the desire for clout may partly explain why so many hacks in recent weeks have targeted retail outlets. The Foschini Group, the South African owner of UK high street brands Hobbs and Whistles, this week announced that some of its IT systems had been hacked. Last week a hacker group called Xuanye managed to hijack the app notification system of Asos, sending a mobile alert to millions of customers in what appears to be an attempt to manufacture maximum fear.
“It helps the threat actors because it’s all extra leverage. They want to put as much pressure as possible on the victim to make them pay,” said Sinnott.

This could soon get a lot more serious. The UK’s AI minister warned this week that it was “likely, if not inevitable” that government systems would be breached, following the incident when a rogue OpenAI agent hacked Australia’s health service in June. Kanishka Narayan says he wants cyber security “discussed in every boardroom in Britain”.

A Lords amendment to the cyber security and resilience bill that is moving through parliament would seek to make senior executives personally liable for penalties if their organisation’s cyber-compliance failure occurred through their “consent, connivance, neglect or carelessness”.

Serious breaches will have to be reported within 24 hours, including overnight and at weekends, and can result in fines of £17m or up to 4% of global turnover, whichever is larger. In July last year the Home Office said it would ban critical infrastructure operators from paying ransoms. Supermarkets would not count as an “essential service” under the bill.

news.title: Health Marine Saint Endometriosis leaves women out of pocket and ‘treated like skivers’ Almost 50% of women with the condition suffer financial hardship, finds new report
text: Kirsteen Sullivan, chair of the parliamentary group on endometriosis
Loneliness influencers have found a viral audience for their solitude
‘A voice told me I was in hell’: the reality of post-partum psychosis
Almost half of working women with endometriosis in the UK have lost income because of the symptoms, research has shown.

Some 47% of women surveyed had lost money, with 40% saying they had suffered financial hardship because of the often painful condition, according to a report released today by the all-party parliamentary group on endometriosis and charity Endometriosis UK. Almost a third of sufferers said they had left a job as a result.

Endometriosis is a chronic condition in which tissue similar to that lining the uterus grows elsewhere in the body, causing often debilitating physical symptoms including pain, stabbing-like pelvic cramps, inflammation and heavy periods. It affects one in 10 women and those assigned female at birth. There is no cure.

It is estimated that at least 1.5 million people live with the condition in the UK, although many cases go undiagnosed and are subject to an average diagnosis time of nine years and four months. The report was largely based on an employee survey that received 6,239 responses.
Laura, 46, waited nearly 30 years between first experiencing symptoms at 13 and receiving an endometriosis diagnosis.

She said the “indescribable pain” of her condition worsened after she stopped taking the birth control pill and became a “really big day-to-day challenge” at her part-time operations job at Transport for London. Laura said she was recently “medically terminated” from her position.

“This is now a very stressful situation financially,” she said. “I’ve done everything in my power to try and deal with the condition, but stress in itself is the worst thing for an inflammatory condition, and this has had a huge impact on why my symptoms have been worse.”

A TfL spokesperson said: “While we cannot comment on an individual case, we actively seek to identify where adjustments for health reasons may support colleagues at work. We will always look to explore all options to help people stay in work, with the aim of assisting employees to remain in or return to work where possible.”
Loneliness influencers have found a viral audience for their solitude
‘A voice told me I was in hell’: the reality of post-partum psychosis

Laura asked to move to a less physically demanding role in the company, but claimed she was refused. She hopes the report will raise awareness – in the government and among employers – about the impact of endometriosis on personal and work life.

She would like there to be a mandatory framework for managers to help them accommodate women with the condition. “It would help stop the discrimination, and women feeling ashamed, embarrassed, disbelieved, not only by employers, but by other colleagues. And that mental health impact cannot be underestimated about not being listened to, believed, treated as though you’re a skiver.”

The inquiry found that endometriosis has a significant, long-term physical and financial impact on working life that is “not always inevitable”, as women “worked through severe pain”, wrote Kirsteen Sullivan, chair of the parliamentary group and Labour MP for Bathgate and Linlithgow. The inquiry launched in March 2026 and now calls for better workplace adjustments, along with “dignity and respect at work”.

Emma Cox, head of Endometriosis UK, said of women with endometriosis that “too often, what stands in their way is not their ability, but a workplace that fails to provide the right support when it is needed”.

The report also asked employers how endometriosis could be better addressed in their workplaces. Of the women surveyed, 79% said current employment law and guidance did not provide sufficient clarity on supporting endometriosis. Only 11% of UK employers have a menstrual health policy, according to software company Ciphr.

The all-party parliamentary group and Endometriosis UK are also campaigning to reduce the diagnosis time to one year by 2030, and have asked the government to implement national guidance and workplace requirements.

Suggested guidelines from Endometriosis UK include flexibility with working hours, shift changes, breaks, paid time for medical appointments and suitable uniforms. The charity also asked for tailored workplace conditions when working from home is impossible.
The Department of Health and Social Care pointed to the renewed women’s health strategy, which identifies endometriosis as a priority condition and commits to improve its treatment.

A department spokesperson said: “This analysis shows exactly why that extra support is so necessary, and that it must not be confined to the healthcare that women with endometriosis receive, but also the accommodations that are made for them in the workplace and in other walks of life.”

news.title: Media Sarah Dear David Sedaris says ‘only losers watch podcasts’. We’re all losers now The pivot to a fully visualised medium is capturing attention and gaming algorithms
text: Why was the ‘most trustworthy’ Faithful banished from Celebrity Traitors?
Aaron Sorkin: the film-maker with a moral conscience taking on Meta

Not long ago, the American humorist and author, David Sedaris, sat on a dusty pink chair, looked directly into the camera lens, and spoke sternly into a microphone: “Anybody watching this at home, you are a loser. Only losers watch podcasts.”

Sedaris was appearing on Elizabeth Day’s prolific How To Fail podcast. Since 2025, episodes have also been published on Day’s YouTube channel, filmed in a maroon-drenched studio with slatted wood walls, fresh flowers and plush cushions, an aesthetic that has become ubiquitous with video podcasting.
“I miss audio-only podcasting,” Day later confessed on LinkedIn. “The fact is, the podcast had to become fully visualised in order to keep up with everyone else in the market.”

Welcome to the vodcast era: where video is overtaking audio as the preferred method of podcast consumption. More than half of UK podcast consumers now prefer video versions, either to watch directly or leave playing in the background, according to Ofcom. This shift in audience demand is forcing an evolution from podcasters – from the intimacy of speaking directly into listeners’ ears to the more glossy production of video.

As vodcasts go mainstream, one format has begun to dominate. A recent survey of 34,000 English-language video podcasts found that 72% focused on interviews or conversations. Among the top 10, more than half resemble a modern-day chatshow, such as The Joe Rogan Experience, Call Her Daddy and The Diary of a CEO.

This era has also ushered in the rise of the celebrity podcast. “There’s still a coolness with podcasts that people want to get in with,” says Richard Berry, a senior lecturer in Radio at Sunderland University. “For celebrities, it could take six months to negotiate a chat show with a broadcaster. With a podcast, they can just go out and do it.”

At the centre of this shift is YouTube, which is now used by 94% of adults in the UK. As YouTube has become highly integrated into daily lives, it has also grown into a major player in the podcast space: it now reports more than 1bn monthly active podcast viewers.

“We bet on the fact that video podcasts would be a thing,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told Semafor. “People would want to not just listen to a conversation… but also see who’s having that conversation and feel part of it.” With this bet, YouTube invested in the vodcast experience: launching a dedicated podcast homepage, offering a new route for discovery through Shorts clips, and using its recommendation algorithms to attract new audiences to the format.
Why was the ‘most trustworthy’ Faithful banished from Celebrity Traitors?
Aaron Sorkin: the film-maker with a moral conscience taking on Meta

As YouTube asserts its dominance over the vodcast market, the platform subtly shifts what gets made. “Reaching audiences on different platforms is a good thing, but you end up trying to chase what the algorithm wants. And no one really knows the answer,” an unnamed podcast producer tells me.

YouTube’s business is built on capturing attention, and attempts to optimise for the algorithm can lead to an eerie homogenisation. When I type “podcast” into a private YouTube search, the result is striking: almost all the thumbnails are two men and an intriguing, emboldened quote against a dark studio backdrop. When I type “podcast women”, the images are similar, but the backgrounds turn to pink.

If podcasts become a vehicle for algorithmic visibility, success depends on capturing attention efficiently. This creates pressure to package shows in particular ways and to produce formats that can be made quickly, on repeat. This means the economics of vodcasting favour conversation: a chat show is usually cheaper and quicker to produce than a complex story or analysis.

“I can’t see it going back to investigative journalism,” the producer tells me. “I don’t see the platforms losing their hold, which means it will stay geared towards chat shows and celebrities.” Narrative and audio-only shows won’t disappear entirely, but YouTube seems to be doing what successful platforms always do: becoming large enough to have its own gravitational pull, reshaping everything in its orbit.

On Monday, the UK’s AI minister Kanishka Narayan warned it was “likely, if not inevitable” that the UK’s cyber defences would be breached at some point, potentially exposing sensitive information. Narayan’s focus now is to identify and fix vulnerabilities across government systems before they can be exploited.

Narayan’s warning comes amid a rise in incidents of AI models “going rogue”, including an OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. The UK has a good reputation when it comes to AI regulation, according to Microsoft president Brad Smith. Smith recently told the BBC that, if you asked people he knew in the tech sector to “name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it’s very simple. It’s the United Kingdom”.

A key component of Narayan’s plan is the AI Security Institute (AISI), the UK’s AI watchdog responsible for testing models before release. However, reports last month that the White House had asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold models from British testers highlights a flaw in AISI’s approach: it depends on the cooperation of foreign governments and big tech companies. Narayan confirmed that the UK now has access to the latest models, but reliable access is essential for the UK to scrutinise the technology properly and drive global regulation.

Narayan might be worrying about fridges, after the news that hundreds of French supermarket chains were hacked over the weekend. The hackers remotely triggered refrigerators to defrost on a slow timer, resulting in food losses and fires.
“We only realized at 4am when our delivery driver saw the storeroom was flooded,” one Intermarché owner told Le Monde. “The temperature had reached 50C in the cold room, which set off a sprinkler.”

According to Le Monde, the manufacturers were aware of the vulnerability in their security systems and had urged its customers to install updates. Yet many supermarkets were still using older software, leaving them vulnerable to attack. The hack is predicted to have cost supermarkets across the country several million euros.

Bumble agreed to a $1.3bn acquisition yesterday, as reported in Semafor. The buyer is Ithaca Holdings, an investment firm recently formed by two Silicon Valley executives. The sale comes amidst the company’s declining revenues and the public’s growing disillusionment with dating apps; at its peak, Bumble was valued at $14bn.

It’s been a tumultuous few years for Bumble. The app originally made its name by nudging women to start conversations, before quietly reversing this tactic in 2024. As my colleague Patricia Clarke reported last year, the company’s pivot was actually a response to ongoing legal pressure from men’s rights activists.

Trump shared real footage of a man being killed by a tiger at South Yorkshire Zoo; he then shared an AI video where he wrestles a tiger. The family have since urged people to stop sharing videos of the attack on social media.

news.title: Economy Ben Zaranko With weeks to go, all signs point to a ‘Phoney Budget’
text: The eight-month period from September 1939 to May 1940, at the beginning of the Second World War, was nicknamed the “Phoney War”. The relative calm and absence of major military operations contributed to a sense of anticlimax and unreality, as the public braced for what was surely to come.

I think we could be in for a “Phoney Budget” on 28 October, one in which virtually all decisions of note are delayed until next year, and we’re left wondering when the government’s efforts to break with the economic policies of the last 40 years will begin in earnest. First, the context…

There is general agreement among analysts that the outlook for UK government borrowing has worsened a bit since the last time official forecasts were produced, in the spring, driven largely by higher interest rates on government debt. That doesn’t mean the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) will necessarily agree. As the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) pointed out this week, forecasts for future borrowing are hugely sensitive to judgments over the path for earnings, and how higher inflation will feed through to different parts of the economy. The OBR may take a sunnier view than others.

But for the sake of argument, let’s assume John Healey has been handed a forecast that says if he does nothing, his buffer – or “headroom”, to use the unhelpful but common parlance – against the fiscal rules has fallen from £24bn in spring to something closer to half that amount. That is, he’s still meeting his rules, and UK government borrowing is still set to fall, but not quite as quickly.

Much of the pre-budget debate has focused on what Healey should do in such a scenario. In an interview with the Financial Times, Jim O’Neill, erstwhile adviser to Andy Burnham, said Healey should meet his rules by a narrower margin rather than impose tax rises to offset any deterioration in the borrowing outlook. O’Neill said: “It’s quite reasonable to have a buffer that you use in an emergency. That’s kind of what it is, when you see what’s going on in the Gulf and with bond yields. I think it’s not just legitimate, but wise.”

It’s a reasonable argument. There is nothing special about a £24bn buffer. Calibrating tax changes to precisely offset a change in the forecast for debt interest spending would be deeply unwise (especially when that forecast is so sensitive to the precise time window when market conditions were measured). Badly designed tax changes could weigh on the UK’s otherwise encouraging economic momentum.

And Healey could argue that the whole point of keeping a buffer against the rules is to absorb unexpected shocks, like a foreign war that pushes up inflation and bond yields. (You may think the fact that unexpected events keep happening is a poor argument for reducing the government’s buffer against uncertainty, but let’s put that to one side for now).

Healey could follow that logic, accept a slower pace of deficit reduction (ie lower “headroom”), and present a straightforward budget that provides some targeted energy price support for the winter, devolves some income tax revenues to mayors, finds £1bn a year for the defence investment plan, and doesn’t do much else. The goal would be to buy some time, in the hope that the outlook improves by next year, and to keep the beady eye of the bond market fixed on the other side of the English channel. It’s probably the safest short-term option, and in a volatile world, there’s something to be said for that.

The forecasts showing the government meeting its fiscal rules would be based on departmental spending plans Rachel Reeves penciled in for the next five years. Towards the back end of the parliament, they always looked implausibly tight, because they imply substantial budget cuts for everything that isn’t the NHS or the Ministry of Defence. Now, given higher inflation (and the resulting pay demands that will generate from public sector unions), they look entirely fanciful. That’s before factoring in the cost of increasing UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, an issue that – lest we forget – Healey resigned over earlier this year. Combined, the IFS estimates that these pressures amount to about £35bn a year by 2030.

There’s nothing to force Healey to face up to this now, and I strongly suspect he won’t. Instead, the big decisions – how to fund higher defence spending, how to reform welfare, how to rebalance the tax system – will probably be pushed into the future. Much of this will come to a head at next year’s spending review, when the government has to set out in black and white how much it plans to spend on defence, the police, the NHS, prisons, and so on. That will be when the phoney war ends, and when the real fighting begins.

I’ve long thought that the 2027 spending review will be the moment of maximum fiscal danger for this government. Negotiations between departments and the Treasury are going to be brutal. There will be huge pressure for the Treasury to increase its so-called “envelope” – the overall spending limits – to accommodate additional requests from departments, and take the sharpest edges off the budgetary trade-offs.

To end on a cynical note, another argument for operating with a smaller buffer against the fiscal rules would be to strengthen the Treasury’s hand in those negotiations. If Healey can say, “Sorry, prime minister, I’d love to spend an extra £10bn, but we just can’t – it would mean breaching our fiscal rules”, he may find it easier to fend off such requests. I doubt he’d give that justification in the Commons, but that doesn’t mean his officials won’t have thought about it.

In a bid to ease cost pressures ahead of the midterms, President Trump signed an executive order last week that temporarily allows red-dyed diesel to be used on American highways. Red diesel (dyed that colour so it can be identified) is exempt from federal excise taxes, and its use is generally limited to farm equipment and other off-road purposes.

In the UK, red diesel is subject to much lower tax than other types (6.48 pence per litre, versus 52.95 pence per litre on road diesel). Its use is strictly limited to qualifying businesses and vehicles. My favourite example? Travelling circuses.

Healey has pledged that he’ll tackle both the cost of living and the cost of business in his upcoming budget. Some British firms feeling the impact of higher fuel costs are urging the chancellor to emulate the Trump administration and allow them to use cheaper red diesel.

Among them is Simon Wilkinson (pictured below), who runs Wilkinsons Landscapes, a landscaping firm in the north-east that operates 30 diesel-powered machines along with a range of road vehicles. “I can’t say I agree with Donald Trump on everything, and in fact the current fuel price issue is largely caused by his actions, but there is a lesson in the approach being taken in America,” says Wilkinson. He wants to see a temporary widening of red diesel access.

“We use the exact same machinery to do the exact same job as many of the sectors which qualify for red diesel, yet we’re excluded because of the industry we’re in … I think most people struggle to understand the logic,” he added.

From an economic perspective, it would make little sense for the government to take measures to encourage businesses to use more diesel in the middle of a global diesel shortage. And the Treasury will be acutely aware that supposedly “temporary” measures to lower the cost of fuel have a habit of becoming permanent. But if the chancellor is looking for ways to reduce the “cost of business”, this is the sort of thing that may come under consideration.
Simon Wilkinson, managing director of Wilkinson Landscapes, is unhappy with the government’s current eligibility criteria for red diesel

The government announced last Thursday that Google Maps will “reflect near real-time prices at the pump for [the] first time”, in a development that Polly Billington, minister for energy consumers, described as a “gamechanger”. The hope is clearly that providing additional information to consumers will drive competition between petrol stations, and bring down costs on the forecourt. Perhaps it will.

But the flipside of information disclosure policies like this is that it also provides near real-time information to each firm’s rivals, which can facilitate coordination or monitoring. A petrol station thinking about cutting its prices knows that the station on the other side of town would be immediately alerted, and may therefore decide that it’s not worth doing so. If their rival will just immediately follow suit to avoid appearing more expensive on Google Maps, perhaps they’ll conclude it’s better just to leave prices where they are.

One study by Fernando Luco, an economics professor at Texas A&M University, found that when the Chilean government introduced an online price disclosure policy in 2012, margins in the retail petrol industry actually increased by an average of 9% for this reason.

It’s a different setting, and it’s easier for customers to search on their phones nowadays, so I’m not sure the UK government’s policy will have the same effect. It does, all the same, make you wonder whether the rush of “retail” policies – government departments have reportedly been tasked with producing one each week – will have unintended consequences.

One of my proudest achievements since starting at The Observer was coming up with the concept of a Richard: someone who Retired In a Comfortable House and Refuses to Downsize. The Richards no doubt looked on approvingly last week as Kemi Badenoch announced that a Conservative government would exempt family homes from inheritance tax: a policy almost perfectly calibrated to discourage downsizing. In their defence, the Conservatives also want to scrap stamp duty, which would encourage more housemoving, but that doesn’t make the inheritance tax policy any better designed.
The Economist made an important new contribution to the lexicon this week with an article on Sue, Henry and Walter.

Sue is a Standard Undertaxed Earner, who is able to enjoy the benefits of state largesse only thanks to the tax contributions of her richer friends – the well-known Henry (High Earner, Not Rich Yet) and the lesser-known Walter (Wealthy Already, Lightly Taxed, Ever Richer). The piece notes that Sue has the votes, Walter has the accountants, and Henry gets unduly punished by the tax system as a result. It’s very good. I wish I’d come up with it.

news.title: Palestine Mishal Khan Palestinians need Britain to act against sexual violence in war
text: ‘After any woman falls to her death, police should think: domestic abuse’

Freedom and safety for women and girls are core to British values. The UK is rightly quick to condemn violations of these principles elsewhere. Sexual violence – typically perpetrated against women and girls but also against men and boys – is a global public health and human rights crisis, rooted in unequal power, discrimination and impunity. Conflict intensifies these conditions, exposing people to abuse while making protection, healthcare and justice harder to access. The consequences include physical injury, psychological trauma, reproductive health problems and lasting harm to families and communities. Sexual violence can also make people feel unsafe in their own homes or force them to leave the places where they have lived for generations.

These harms are not inevitable. Governments can help prevent them by recognising warning signs, protecting civilians and holding perpetrators accountable. The UK has admirably committed to “drive global efforts” against conflict-related sexual violence. Yet when it comes to sexual violence against Palestinians, the UK and international response remains profoundly inadequate.

We have allowed thousands of Palestinians, including children, to be killed on the grounds that they were terrorists or might become terrorists. We have allowed hospitals and refugee camps to be bombed on the grounds that they were harbouring terrorists. But no claim of counterterrorism can justify sexual abuse of children, sexualised torture of prisoners or rape threats against women and girls at checkpoints. Such abuses demand independent investigation, accountability and a decisive international response.

In a recent article in the British Medical Journal, I joined colleagues in examining evidence of sexual violence against Palestinian women, men, girls and boys. Reports from United Nations investigations, medical professionals and humanitarian and human rights organisations document widespread sexual violence and humiliation in detention, during raids and at checkpoints, as well as in the context of displacement. They also highlight the barriers survivors face in reporting abuse and accessing independent investigations.
These accounts demand more than expressions of concern. They require action to prevent further harm and ensure accountability.

The UK government has repeatedly stated that preventing sexual violence in conflict is a priority. Through its Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict Initiative, it supports efforts to document abuses, improve survivor support and strengthen accountability. Its commitments to gender equality and the Women, Peace and Security agenda recognise that conflict affects people differently and that protection must be central to peace and security.

At the UN security council, the UK has expressed alarm about conflict-related sexual violence, including reports concerning Palestinian detainees, and called for investigations and accountability. The UK has also begun taking more concrete action. Sanctions against individuals linked to settler violence and measures targeting illegal settlement activity are important steps towards addressing impunity. They show that the government can move beyond condemnation and use its influence to respond to abuses against Palestinians. This progress should be recognised. But it must form part of a wider approach that addresses sexual violence and the conditions in which it occurs.

The West Bank shows why prevention matters. Research published in April by the West Bank Protection Consortium examines how sexual violence, sexualised humiliation and other forms of gender-based abuse contribute to the conditions forcing Palestinian communities from their homes. Among households that answered a relevant question, more than 70 per cent identified violence against women and children as a decisive factor in their decision to leave.
‘After any woman falls to her death, police should think: domestic abuse’

International humanitarian law prohibits sexual violence and protects civilians under occupation. It also prohibits forcible transfer, including where coercive conditions leave people with no genuine choice but to leave. The UK and other states must respect and help ensure respect for these protections. The International Court of Justice’s 2024 advisory opinion made clear that states must not recognise as lawful or assist in maintaining Israel’s unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory, and must cooperate through lawful means to bring it to an end.

For the UK, this means examining whether its policies help prevent harm. Arms transfers, trade, investment and diplomatic cooperation must be assessed against the risk of contributing to serious violations. It also means pressing for independent investigations, protecting access for medical and humanitarian organisations, and ensuring survivors can access confidential healthcare and psychosocial support. Women and girls must not be overlooked, nor should men and boys, whose experiences of sexual violence can be particularly difficult to disclose.

The UK has recognised that preventing sexual violence in conflict requires more than condemnation. Its recent measures show that it can use its influence to address abuses against Palestinians. It must now apply that resolve consistently, ensuring that credible reports of sexual violence prompt independent investigation and that survivors receive protection and support.

Palestinians deserve the same protection and accountability that the UK promises to people affected by sexual violence everywhere. The test of Britain’s commitment and leadership is whether it acts on those principles when they are most difficult to uphold.
Photograph by Mosab Shawer/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
Mishal Khan is professor of global public health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

news.title: Violence against women Louise Tickle ‘After any woman falls to her death, police should think: domestic abuse’
text: Are French supermarket fridge hackers just shopping for kudos?

Killing someone by pushing them off a balcony or out of a window is a type of homicide that can very easily be hidden. It is also a type of homicide that is easy not to see, if police officers who arrive at the scene fail to ask the right questions.

Jhiselle Feanny, a domestic abuse campaigner whose sister, Bianca Thomas, died after falling from her ex-boyfriend’s 11th-floor flat, is convinced that more abused women are being pushed to their deaths than police forces currently recognise or investigate. Thomas’s ex was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder, then released with no further action taken. He has consistently denied involvement in her death. A coroner found that Thomas fell while intoxicated and recorded a verdict of accidental death.

As co-founder of the charity Killed Women, Feanny is urging national police chiefs to change the way forces approach fall deaths by adopting as standard an investigatory protocol, “Bee’s law”, named for her sister. This would require officers to be curious about every fall from height, and to investigate whether the victim had been subjected to domestic abuse in the run-up to their death.

“We’ve been able to establish that 31 of the 39 women who fell to their deaths over the past five years had domestic abuse markers against their names or their partners’ on police systems,” says Feanny. “That means all falls should be treated as suspicious, especially when it’s a woman.”
There have been no successful murder prosecutions in England and Wales after a woman has died by falling.

“A precautionary approach would mean evidence wasn’t discarded that can’t be recreated later,” Feanny points out. A woman’s vulnerability, such as being drunk or taking drugs, also wouldn’t automatically be used to explain the fall. “And a single account from a man who was at the scene wouldn’t be allowed to become the dominant narrative if independent witnesses didn’t corroborate what he said.”
Adopting a precautionary approach to fall deaths could lead to more dangerous abusers being charged and jailed, thus protecting future victims.

This has already started to happen with suicide deaths. Police and prosecutors now better understand that the decision to take one’s own life can be substantially influenced by the experience of domestic abuse.
Are French supermarket fridge hackers just shopping for kudos?

An upcoming documentary presented by Stacey Dooley, Fallen Women – inspired by original reporting from The Slow Newscast podcast – explores the recent death in Scotland of Kimberly Milne, who leapt off a road bridge into oncoming traffic. It seemed an obvious suicide, until police looked into the context of her death and discovered that Milne had been subjected to sustained domestic abuse by her husband.

Earlier this year Lee Milne was put on trial for culpable homicide (similar to manslaughter in English law). He was found guilty by the jury and jailed for eight years. He is appealing his conviction.

Feanny points to the fact that in England and Wales, police now have the ability to classify a suicide death as “suspected domestic abuse-related”. The number of suicides with this marker increased from 68 recorded cases in 2020-21 to 150 in 2024-25. She believes the same trend could be seen with fall deaths if police adopted Bee’s Law. “A freedom of information request to 44 police forces came back with just one of them saying it had a ‘fall from height’ marker available on its system,” she says. Nine had no marker, and the other forces either couldn’t or didn’t answer.

National policy now requires officers to check for signs of domestic abuse when attending all sudden and unexpected deaths, including falls from height, according to Louisa Rolfe, the National Police Chiefs’ Council national lead for domestic abuse. “Our deep-dive assessments have shown this has led to further investigation,” she says. “This isn’t limited to ‘markers’ on police systems but also listening to friends and family.”

Findings from the Home Office-funded Domestic Homicide Project have already driven change, she adds, including “training for officers to raise awareness of the link between domestic abuse and suicide, and changing policy to ensure there are explicit procedures to prompt officers to consider domestic abuse in unexpected deaths or suspected suicides, and carry out system checks”.

In memory of her sister, and on behalf of Thomas’s three children, Feanny has pledged never to stop campaigning for better investigation of fall deaths. “Lots of elderly people are falling on stairs with their partners there,” she said. “That’s expected. But what if it’s something else? That’s the next thing to look at.”
Stacey Dooley: Fallen Women is available on iPlayer from Tuesday 13 October. Listen to the original Slow Newscast investigation, Fallen Women, here.
What are your thoughts on this? Email us at letters@observer.co.uk

news.title: Body politic Eva Wiseman Loneliness influencers have found a viral audience for their solitude
text: A little loneliness can be painful – the level of pain perhaps that of a blister, a paper cut or a bruise. A lot of loneliness, however, has the ability to kill.

In Zoë Heller’s novel Notes on a Scandal the narrator, Barbara, describes the “drip, drip of long-haul, no-end-in-sight solitude”, of sitting alone on trains “feeling the great store of unused, objectless love sitting in my belly like a stone”. It’s a cancer, a haemorrhage, an alarm.

Long-term isolation increases the risk of premature death by 26%, similar to the effect of smoking, and raises the risk of stroke by 32%. We know this. We know about the “loneliness epidemic”, a phrase that has always jarred with me as it suggests, doesn’t it, something spread by human contact. And we know about the government initiatives and, more recently, the industries replacing people with programs, and the rise of AI companions who say they see you.

A few years ago I visited a robotics lab in Bristol where they had built a little bungalow right in the centre and populated it with jazzy technology designed for the elderly. It was a time when we still marvelled at robot vacuum cleaners and had the time to interrogate the boundaries of our own humanness. There was one robot with a tablet in place of a chest that displayed family photographs, intended to be a companion for people with dementia. They called it Molly. I left the lab believing this robot, with its big painted eyes, was the cure for loneliness, that this was the future. And then there was the pandemic, and then ChatGPT was released, and then here we are.
The women taking on the tech giants over deepfakes and digital abuse

It makes sense that attention is paid to loneliness when it reaches crisis levels, but there are infinite textures to our relationship with solitude that are no less interesting, all of which threaten to teach us something about how to be human. Perhaps the most vivid (but least critical) scholars of loneliness are those who look at it through their camera lens.

“Loneliness influencers”, as they’ve come to be known, share videos of themselves in anonymous new-build apartments, typically disinfecting their shoes, preparing ready meals and wiping down countertops, with the caption: “POV you’re single, have no friends, live alone and won’t be having kids, so this is your Friday night.” Hundreds of thousands follow for updates on these women’s routines, frequently commenting with details from their own solitary lives, and in doing so creating communities in which, ironically, they honour their individual lonelinesses.

Of course, the more I lingered on these videos, the more these videos were presented to me, and the more I started to wonder about what, or who, they were for. Much in the way the audience for tradwife content seems largely to be made up of feminists gawping judgily, with moments of envy, I suspect many of those watching loneliness influencers are busy caregivers craving a moment alone.

Is the influencer documenting their neat, silent life in order to hold it at a remove and reimagine it as a performance? Or are they filming to make it more real, to watch it back as evidence of survival? Are they sharing it to alleviate the very loneliness they’ve glamourised? Could they (gasp!) be just like all the other influencers, only showing the internet an edited version of a life that’s far more chaotic and populated behind the scenes? And what does it tell us about loneliness itself?

For all we know about loneliness, whether through science or art, it’s clear there is always more to learn. I find myself thinking of its opposite: the feeling of “being seen”, a phrase beloved of podcasters, which can flatten an experience (togetherness) that has just as much nuance and complexity as loneliness itself. As the influencers understand, being in the world among other people is difficult and risky, as is the occasional dawn realisation that, even if we create families and find friends, we may never be fully known.

Sometimes the pain of loneliness can be a positive thing, like a hunger or thirst, in that its discomfort spurs us out into the world. Or, perhaps, into a phone. While remaining “unseen”, these influencers have made stars of themselves, with short films for an audience that lusts for solitude but can only grab those moments scrolling strange apartments online. While empathising with those struggling alone, perhaps we should spare a thought, too, for those struggling together.

news.desc: Russia ⁠struck a number ⁠of ​energy facilities ⁠in ⁠Ukraine overnight

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Volodymyr Zelensky said “people were killed” as Starlink went down as he criticised Donald Trump and Elon Musk in a new interview.
The Ukrainian leader hit back after Elon Musk said that usage of Starlink couldn’t be used for offensive military actions as Ukraine faced restrictions on the software.

Appearing on Piers Morgan Uncensored, he said: “It's not about attacks It's also about defending the lives. So people were killed because [there was] not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work, of course.”
He continued that Vladimir Putin was “laughing” and he felt “betrayed” by Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
“It is a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Mr Zelensky said. “Now Putin is laughing because, I mean, this is for him, simple victory – this diesel deal.”
Russia has meanwhile suggested it does not understand the terms of Donald Trump’s supposed energy ceasefire in Ukraine, after continuing to bomb cities and energy plants.
"What is the outline of the energy ceasefire, and what does it mean? Has it been specified?" Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told journalists.
Ukraine’s president has said it’s impossible to do an election as a point of security with drones swarming the country.

Responding to comments by Donald Trump and Elon Musk that he should step down, Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Each hour we have attacks. This massive attack that we discussed, it was about night. But during the day, the same drones are here; hundreds and thousands each hour attack. So that's why, from a security, you can't do elections.
“Then soldiers are on the front. We can't choose the president without soldiers because they give and gave their lives. They are the first who have to vote, and I think it's fair.”
Volodymyr Zelensky has said people were killed while Starlink has been down because they were unable to intercept drones.

“We use drones with Starlink,” he told Piers Morgan. “So it's not about just just attack, as as I said, we didn't didn't attack their energy. It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives.”
Elon Musk said on X that Starlink usage was limited to civilian or defensive activities and could not be used for offensive military action.
Mr Zelensky added: “So people were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work, of course.”
Volodymyr Zelensky described the energy ceasefire as “the worst version of peace.”

He told Piers Morgan: “They wanted us not to attack diesel. My opinion was it's not fair. Energy ceasefire, it's okay, t's understandable. I mean, it's the worst version of peace. But anyway, it's some steps to the peace.”
He continued: “We support it because we need our people to live to go through this winter and to stop the war. This is what we want.”
A Ukrainian presidential adviser denied on Wednesday Russian statements that Kyiv's military struck Russian refineries earlier in the day.
Dmytro Lytvyn told reporters that Ukraine struck a data centre and another unnamed target but not refineries.
Elon Musk responded to Ukraine’s former ministry of defence as Starlink and Starshield are down in the nation.

Mykhailo Fedorov said on X: “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense. Thank you, @elonmusk. We hope for your continued support.”
Responding, Musk said that the Trump controls Starshield systems while Starlink was only for defensive activities, as he implied that it was being used for offensive action.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX.
“Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Wednesday that Ukraine attacked two oil refineries during the day, in Saratov and Ryazan regions.
"We see no indication that the Ukrainian side is moving towards an energy ceasefire," he said.
Andy Burnham pledged that Britain’s support for Ukraine “will not change” as he welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday.

The Ukrainian president received an unprecedented honour guard on his arrival at No 10, made up of troops from the Irish Guards, amid what the Prime Minister described as “dark and difficult days” for his country.
Mr Burnham told Mr Zelensky: “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain.

news.desc: She allegedly obtained approximately $14.7 million from one bank and defrauded other financial institutions

She allegedly obtained approximately $14.7 million from one bank and defrauded other financial institutions
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A 75-year-old woman who allegedly posed as an heiress has been added to the FBI's new Most Wanted Fraudsters list after being accused of defrauding banks in Los Angeles and Orange counties out of millions of dollars.
A reward of $150,000 is available for information resulting in the arrest and conviction of Mary Carole McDonnell, who is also wanted on identity theft charges.

According to Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office Patrick Grandy, McDonnell extracted roughly $14.7 million from a single bank alongside defrauding other financial institutions.
"McDonnell has falsely claimed to be an heiress to the McDonnell aircraft family, with an $80 million secret trust to which she will have access," the FBI said in a statement.

"In December 2018, a federal arrest warrant was issued for McDonnell in the United States District Court, Central District of California, Santa Ana, California, after she was charged with bank fraud and aggravated identity theft. It is believed McDonnell is currently in Dubai."
She is reported to have used several aliases, including Mary Carole Carroll, Mary Carol McDonnell, Mary Carroll McDonnell, Mary C. Carroll, and Mary Carroll McDonald.

McDonnell is described as white, 5-feet-7 inches tall, weighing approximately 145 pounds, with blond hair, blue eyes, and a scar on her right knee. The FBI noted her physical appearance may have altered over the years.
She maintains personal or professional ties to Los Angeles, Montgomery, Alabama, and Dubai, United Arab Emirates.
"McDonnell is wanted for defrauding financial institutions out of millions and is known to have falsified her inheritance and background," Grandy said.

"It's just a matter of time before McDonnell is caught as we work with our international partners to locate her. A generous reward is being offered in exchange for information leading to her apprehension and conviction, and a tip from the public might break the case."

Authorities say McDonnell launched the now-defunct Burbank television production and distribution outfit Bellum Entertainment in 2004, which originally operated as LongNeedle Entertainment and focused on true crime stories.
Designed specifically to target fugitives sought for major financial crimes, the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters list operates independently from the agency's well-known Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.
Anyone possessing details regarding McDonnell's current whereabouts is asked to notify their regional FBI office or the closest American Embassy or Consulate.
Alternatively, individuals can call the FBI's toll-free line at 1-80-ALL- FBI or submit information online at tips.fbi.gov.

Six people, including one child, were killed in a plane crash in Wisconsin on Tuesday night after the pilot reported that ice was accumulating on the wings during a thunderstorm, authorities reported.

The single-engine, six-seat plane was en route from Kenosha to Menomonie when it crashed shortly before 10 p.m. in a wooded area near Mirror Lake State Park, not far from Wisconsin Dells, the Sauk County Sheriff’s Department said. Rain was falling as a thunderstorm moved through the Town of Dellona.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the pilot notified an air traffic controller of wing icing on the Piper PA-46 at 24,000 feet (7,315 meters) and asked for clearance to descend. Ice buildup is a severe aviation hazard because even a thin layer can make it difficult for an aircraft to stay airborne.
Air traffic control approved the request, and the aircraft entered a right descending turn that increased in rate until radio contact and tracking data were lost, according to the NTSB.

The Sauk County Sheriff’s Department reported receiving multiple calls of a downed aircraft. No buildings were damaged, and no injuries were reported on the ground. The names of the five adults and child who died aboard the plane were not immediately released.

The NTSB is leading the investigation into the site, situated roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) west of Wisconsin Dells. The area promotes itself as the “Waterpark Capital of the World” owing to its concentration of parks, attracting more than 5 million visitors in 2025, according to state tourism figures.

news.desc: Pennsylvania has reported six deaths due to measles this year
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Pennsylvania has reported six deaths due to measles this year
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The Trump administration is sending a disease detective to Pennsylvania after the state requested help in fighting its worst outbreak of measles in 35 years.
Six people have died from the highly-contagious illness there in the past three months, including two infants, and cases have ballooned to 1,136.
Pennsylvania formally requested assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, CDC spokesman Gabriel Alvarado told The Independent.

“Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Schwartz continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection. CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” Alvarado said Wednesday.

A CDC disease detective - a scientist specifically trained to handle epidemics - is expected to arrive later this week. The CDC is also providing nearly $4 million to help the state battle the outbreak.
The state’s health department did not immediately return a request for comment.

Pennsylvania’s Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro previously blasted what he called the Trump administration’s “incompetence” in responding to measles. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., a known vaccine skeptic, has previously claimed that Pennsylvania’s measles death toll was “fabricated.”
Nationwide, cases of measles are also at their highest levels in 35 years which public health officials told The Independent was down to vaccine hesitancy and misinformation.

Some 157 cases of measles have been reported in Pennsylvania in the last week. A measles case reported by Georgia health officials Tuesday was also tied to the Pennsylvania outbreak. More than 4,000 infections have been reported in nearly every state in the contiguous U.S. this year, according to the latest CDC data.
The official CDC measles death count stands at two this year - four fewer than Pennsylvania’s official count. The CDC says the data will be updated based on new information and “relevant reviews.”

Measles infections can be prevented with the MMR vaccine, which target measles, mumps and rubella. Two shots offer lifelong protection against severe illness. Without the shots, measles can cause life-threatening brain swelling, high fever, pneumonia and death.
It has been decades since the last time measles ripped through the country in the same way and fewer people are getting vaccinated.

“I think that not only did we eliminate the disease, we eliminated the memory of the disease. I think people don’t remember measles,” Dr. Paul Offit, an infectious disease expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, previously told The Independent.

news.title: Yemen's Houthis are reframing 'Iran proxy' role as they bring war to Saudi Arabia
news.desc: The evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
The evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.

As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.

The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.

It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.

What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.

When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.

But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.

Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.

Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.

During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.

The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.

From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.

After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.

The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.

The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.

Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.

These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.

With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.

This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.

It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.

Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.
