news.title: MAGA is defending Trump’s new press secretary. His staff isn’t convinced
news.desc: Insiders worry that Trump’s snap decision to select Zacharia against the advice of his chief of staff echoes mistakes of his first term, writes Andrew Feinberg
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Insiders worry that Trump’s snap decision to select Zacharia against the advice of his chief of staff echoes mistakes of his first term, writes Andrew Feinberg
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Three days into her tenure as White House Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia’s shaky performance at her debut briefing is testing the Trump White House’s MAGA messaging machine and exposing divisions within the administration not seen since the chaotic days of President Donald Trump’s first term.

Zacharia, a Pepperdine law school graduate and ubiquitous television commentator who reportedly sought out the press secretary role by timing her appearances on right-wing networks to when she believed Trump would be watching, left reporters stunned on Wednesday when her initial appearance in the White House briefing room lasted just 14 minutes.

The neophyte spokesperson spent eight minutes of that reading — haltingly — from a scripted statement before she took softball questions from three conservative-leaning outlets and made a hasty exit after confusing the president with her husband and announcing the firing of Trump’s U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
The White House’s public messaging kicked into gear immediately thereafter, with Communications Director Stephen Cheung posting on X that Zacharias’ debut was “a tremendous start.”
“She commanded the room and effectively reminded the American people of all the great work President Trump and his Administration has done thus far,” Cheung insisted.

The White House’s official X account similarly described the performance as “a commanding inaugural press briefing,” and President Trump offered praise a short time later when he told reporters: “I thought she was very good.”

Defenders of the administration fanned out across social media and television throughout Tuesday evening and Wednesday, if not to praise Zacharia’s performance than at least to savage her critics as biased — or worse.
Former Pennsylvania senator Rick Santorum, now a paid contributor on Newsmax, said on Wednesday that Zacharia was “not even close to being the worst” White House spokesperson he has seen.

Santorum mocked liberal commentators and late-night television hosts for mocking her performance and suggested that they were attacking the new press secretary because she is white, comparing the criticism to Democrats’ defense of Zacharia’s Biden-era predecessor, Karine Jean-Pierre.

“The people you just saw there commenting on Katie were just rallying behind Karine because she was a DEI hire,” he said. “As long as you’re a DEI hire, you get supported, but if you’re a blonde, white female you get trashed.”

Fox News host Sean Hannity also invoked Jean-Pierre, who was routinely disparaged by Republicans during her tenure, and complained that Zacharia “has been mocked, attacked over her appearance, her hair, the way she spoke” and questioned about her legal credentials by people who once defended the former Biden spokesperson.
But inside Trumpworld, the view of Zacharia is less than glowing.

One former Trump administration official who remains close to people serving in the administration texted The Independent to declare Zacharia’s debut “a train wreck” after previously describing her as a “joke hire” who’d likely be “gone in six months.”

Another insider, a current West Wing denizen, said Zacharia’s outing in the briefing room on Tuesday was “beyond brutal” and suggested that she’ll be on a short leash and will either dramatically improve rapidly or see herself out of the job she campaigned for so effectively.

In addition to the discomfort within the West Wing over the new press secretary’s dismal debut, there is also a growing sense of unease among administration officials over Trump’s decision to cut his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, out of the loop during the hiring process.

Since Karoline Leavitt’s departure, The Independent understands that Wiles was attempting to entice CNN commentator Scott Jennings, the network’s high-profile Trump defender, to replace Leavitt in order to keep the press secretary’s job in the hands of someone who is polished, professional, and understands the complexity of the role.

Not only does a press secretary need to be able to duke it out with reporters in the briefing room, he or she is also tasked with running a large staff who respond to press inquiries at all hours, advising the president and keeping abreast of what is happening behind the scenes.

Leavitt, who had been a low-level staffer in the first Trump White House’s press office, was able to carry out each of those tasks and keep a level of civility in the relations between the press corps and the administration.
But Trump struck when Wiles was out of pocket, making the snap decision to hire Zacharia late last week despite her utter lack of experience in anything except defending him on television.
One veteran of the first Trump White House compared the move to a similar situation during his first term, when Trump was picking a replacement for his second press secretary, Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
During her nearly two years on the job, Sanders had brought in a longtime associate, Hogan Gidley, to be her principal deputy — and presumed successor.
Gidley, a former local television newsman, was generally liked by members of the press corps and understood the nuances of the relationship between reporters and the press office.
But Trump instead installed Stephanie Grisham, then the first lady’s top spokesperson, in the role.

Grisham never held a single briefing, and Gidley, following the snub, moved over to a role in Trump’s doomed re-election campaign. And without an effective spokesperson or a functioning press operation, Trump’s approval ratings continued to tumble heading into a pivotal election.
Quoting Yankees great Yogi Berra, the aide told The Independent that today’s situation feels a lot like the first term.

news.title: Trump insider gets lucrative job picking which acts will perform at the Kennedy Center
news.desc: His compensation package was not disclosed but a job posting for the role indicated a salary range of $270,000-$290,000

His compensation package was not disclosed but a job posting for the role indicated a salary range of $270,000-$290,000
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The Kennedy Center, which is largely closed for renovations, has named a Trump insider as its new artistic director, according to a report.
Rick Canny, who has served as a senior adviser to the performing arts institution since last year, has been appointed to the role in a “consulting capacity,” The Washington Post reported Wednesday.
His compensation package was not disclosed but a job posting for the role indicated a salary range of $270,000-$290,000.

Canny, a veteran entertainment industry executive, has been involved in several efforts to reshape the center since Trump became chair of its board, including a proposal to revamp its ticketing system.

“We need to stop ‘short order cooking’ and get to the renovations,” he wrote in a March email to the center’s chief financial officer, according to the Post. “We don’t need passion projects. This is business.”
Trump took control of the Kennedy Center after becoming chair of its board in February 2025, replacing trustees and installing allies in senior roles.

His board later voted to add his name to the institution, prompting a lawsuit from Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat, and other legal challenges. In May, a district judge ruled that Congress — not the president or board — controlled the center’s name and ordered Trump’s name removed.
In June, workers removed the lettering spelling out Trump’s name from the facade, and a large tarp was then installed in the area.

The president has also championed a two-year closure of the performing arts center, which he says is necessary to make long-overdue renovations. Though the closure has been temporarily blocked by a court, officials announced last month that the center would shut down, citing the need for structural repairs.
The upheaval has coincided with financial strain, which deepened after Trump’s name was added to the building.
Artists canceled performances, and internal projections in May indicated the center would generate $124 million out of the $220 million that had been budgeted for the year.

news.title: Group of men cheered as woman was sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago frat house party: report
news.desc: Friend of alleged victim reported hearing crowd of men outside basement bathroom saying 'When’s it my turn?’ and ‘I want to go in there'
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Friend of alleged victim reported hearing crowd of men outside basement bathroom saying 'When’s it my turn?’ and ‘I want to go in there'
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A group of men cheered as a 21-year-old woman was sexually assaulted in the bathroom of a University of Chicago frat house this past weekend while her two friends frantically tried to pick the lock to rescue her, according to reports.

The woman, 21, reported that she was sexually assaulted by a man at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house at 5625 S. University Ave., around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Chicago Police Department confirmed to The Independent.

Two of her friends told police that a group tried to stop them from entering the bathroom after the men were seen “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.

University of Chicago, one of the U.S.’s top colleges, told The Independent that “a person of interest has been identified.” No arrests have been reported, and the individual has not been publicly identified.

There has been a nationwide reckoning over sexual assault on college campuses after a civil lawsuit was filed last month by a Jane Doe alleging that she had been gang-raped by seven fraternity members at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024.
According to the new Chicago police report, the woman and two friends attended a party at Alpha Epsilon Pi after seeing the event advertised on Instagram, the New York Times reported.

The three women were dancing in the frat’s basement when the alleged victim began kissing a man. One of the friends, who spoke with the Times, lost track of them briefly but then found a small group of men cheering outside a locked bathroom in the basement.
“They were saying things like, ‘When’s it my turn?’ and ‘I want to go in there,’” she said. According to the police report, the group told her it wasn’t her friend inside.

However, when she forced her way in by picking the door lock, she found her friend partially undressed and slumped on the floor. The man had his hands on the alleged victim’s wrists, and she began to say “make it stop” and “get me out of here,” the friend told the newspaper.
The police report said that when one of the women’s friend told the man to get off her, he “responded that everything was ‘cool,’ as though nothing had occurred.”
The woman and her friends later confronted the man outside the frat house and he said they “had identified the wrong person.” He pointed them in another direction and ran off, per the report.

One of the friends tried to chase him, but ran into a police officer and reported the alleged assault, according to the report. The 21-year-old was then hospitalized, police confirmed to The Independent.

The woman is not a student at the University of Chicago, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. She did not return the newspaper’s request for comment, but one of her friends told the paper she was “obviously shaken up” and worried about her name getting out.
The Chicago Maroon, the university’s student newspaper, published an article Tuesday describing a video shared to TikTok that appears to show the alleged perpetrator.

“He f****** assaulted my friend in the bathroom of the f****** frat party. You record all the s*** you want,” an individual who refers to themselves as the alleged victim’s friend, says in the video, which has been shared online. “I walked in there, you f****** took her clothes off.”
On the video, the man can be heard responding, “she wanted to."
Police said the man is 5 feet 7 inches tall with curly hair. He was wearing a black, short-sleeve shirt with black pants at the time of the alleged assault, according to the police report.
An alert from the University of Chicago said the suspect is not affiliated with the school. He was not named in the alert because he has not been charged with a crime.

“This identification has been corroborated by key witness statements and video evidence from University cameras and license plate readers, all of which has been shared with [the Chicago Police Department] by the Department of Safety & Security,” the university alert said.

The university’s chapter of Alpha Epsilon Pi said in a statement on Instagram that no one affiliated with the fraternity was “involved or complicit with this incident.” The chapter says it is working with authorities.
The fraternity’s national chapter told The Independent in a statement, “There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this asault or were aware of it while it was transpiring.”
The spokesperson noted that they do not believe the men “cheering on” the attack were part of the fraternity. They said the fraternity members are fully cooperating with authorities.

Cornell’s Jane Doe lawsuit alleges she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024. None of the men have been criminally charged. All have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell announced this week that it has banned fraternity parties for the rest of the year.

Earlier this month, the Ivy League school appointed former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent investigation into how the school handles sexual assault cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has also assigned state Attorney General Letita James to the case as special prosecutor in a criminal investigation.

After Doe reported the alleged rape in 2024, Cornell began an investigation, which involved multiple hearings and resulted in the suspensions and expulsions of some of the students involved. The Chi Phi fraternity was also shut down.

“Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” the university said in a previous statement. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”

op.title: Trump is abandoning Ukraine to its bleakest winter yet
op.desc: Editorial: Battered by President Putin’s war of terror and apparently losing crucial support from US intelligence and Elon Musk’s Starlink, Kyiv’s brave citizens are closer to cracking than they have been since the start of the war
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Editorial: Battered by President Putin’s war of terror and apparently losing crucial support from US intelligence and Elon Musk’s Starlink, Kyiv’s brave citizens are closer to cracking than they have been since the start of the war
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Russian assault on Ukraine is now well into its fifth bloody year. It is increasingly moving off the battlefields of Donbas, where, despite great numerical superiority, Vladimir Putin’s army is making little – if any – progress against its smaller but braver and more professional enemy.

Instead, the Kremlin’s strategy is increasingly to wage a war of terror against the civilian population of Ukraine. It is cruel and cowardly, violating the rules of war and international conventions. But such concerns have never troubled President Putin.

Ukraine is, to all intents and purposes, actually winning the war on the ground, gaining territory and certainly in no danger of being routed by the Russians. Yet the fear, especially as the capital Kyiv becomes a renewed focus of the attacks, is that the resolve of the Ukrainian people will crack under the pressure, forcing Volodymyr Zelensky’s government to capitulate.
That is why this apparent sickening betrayal of the Ukrainians by the Trump administration and Elon Musk is so terribly tragic and sad.

There may be some technical reasons why US intelligence about Russian incoming aerial bombardments failed to reach the Ukrainian authorities in time to sound the air raid alerts. There may also be some innocent explanation for the partial loss of Ukrainian access to Mr Musk’s Starlink satellites over Russian territory.

Yet at any rate, even as a coincidence, the events of the past 48 hours have rendered Ukrainian cities and their residents – non-combatants in every sense – virtually defenceless in the face of Russian aggression. To use the cliche, such matters are gamechangers. If Kyiv really has lost the support of the Americans in sharing intelligence and guiding Ukrainian counterattacks against Russian strategic military and infrastructure, it becomes far more difficult to hold the Russians back on the domestic front as Ukraine’s cities are pummelled day after day, week after week without an end in sight.

Even if the Europeans wished to – and their resolve has sometimes been found wanting – they simply lack the intelligence networks and missile defence systems that the Ukrainian side so desperately needs to ameliorate and survive these onslaughts.

Whether Donald Trump understands this, or cares, must be in doubt. He seems once more to have fallen more completely under the spell of President Putin, to whom he has expressed public gratitude for the “diesel deal”, a politically helpful symbolic move for the Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, even if it will not cut the cost of fuel much – if at all.

Indeed, Mr Trump seems to have returned to his default view that Mr Zelensky is the problem, and that Ukraine should “get itself a new president”. In return, Mr Putin displays contempt for America by immediately and persistently violating the “energy ceasefire” Mr Trump has been trying to impose on both sides.

Yet the continuing Russian destruction of civilian power supplies in Ukraine passes without any rebuke from the White House. It seems not to have occurred to Mr Trump that such humiliation of his country by the Kremlin might go down badly even among his Maga base (especially if the price of diesel doesn’t soon dive sharply downwards, which it won’t). Mr Trump looks like a dupe as well as callous.

Almost from the earliest days of Mr Putin’s “special military operation”, terror has been part of Russian strategy, up to and including the abduction of Ukrainian children. Apartment blocks have long been a favourite target for Russian drones and missiles. It has never been random. It is worse than that. Once again, as a long and bitter winter approaches, Russia is targeting supplies of domestic gas, electricity and water, and doing so on an unprecedented scale.

All of this will be made far worse if US intelligence and satellite access continue to be denied. The ultimate disaster of defeat for Ukraine edges closer, even without their troops surrendering an inch of territory. One hope is that the few Western leaders Mr Trump still has time for, such as Giorgia Meloni of Italy, can persuade him to change course; or that a change in control of Congress after the 3 November elections can force him into a rethink, starting with the cancellation of the Russian diesel deal, which remains unlawful under the recently passed Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Gestures of solidarity, such as Andy Burnham’s invitation to President Zelensky to visit Downing Street, are valuable but need to be backed by tangible military and financial aid.

Perhaps somebody close to Mr Trump – his son-in-law and chief negotiator Jared Kushner, or the First Lady – will convince him that his best chance of a Nobel Peace Prize is to stop talking about ending wars, and actually make the Russians stop their murderous destruction of the Ukrainian nation.
The more likely outcome is the bleakest winter for the people of Ukraine since this war began. It will take all their spirit to get through it, but they know that occupation would be worse.

op.title: Voices: Andy Burnham celebrates The Independent’s 40th anniversary
op.desc: Prime minister Andy Burnham celebrates The Independent’s 40th anniversary in a letter to Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig
text: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in
Prime minister Andy Burnham celebrates The Independent’s 40th anniversary in a letter to Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

I wanted to write to congratulate you – and everyone who has ever been a part of the Independent – on reaching such an incredible milestone. Forty years is a fantastic achievement; the type we could only dream of in politics!

When the paper was founded in 1986, it was built around an idea that I carry close to me today: independence of mind. It means a lot to me personally because, forty years on, we need that spirit now more than ever.

I have long believed that too much power in this country has been held by too few people, in too few places. That Westminster has become too closed in on itself, and too easily consumed by conversations that mean nothing to the people it is meant to serve. So there is something I particularly admire - something I relate to, even - about the Independent’s history of challenging the status quo, even when it might have been easier to go along with the crowd.

But you have also shown that independence does not mean an absence of values. Over four decades, this newspaper has stood up for democracy, human rights and Britain’s place in the world. It has consistently sought out different points of view and always strived to give people pause for thought over a pat on the back.

That matters hugely today. At a time when trust in our politics is at its lowest and algorithms can push our children into echo chambers with just a couple of swipes, we need journalism that opens up debate rather than shuts it down. We need media outlets that are prepared to challenge views, challenge politicians, and, yes, challenge me. And we need people who are brave enough to go against the grain.
So a happy 40th birthday to everybody at The Independent – and here’s to the next forty.
